lessons.title: The complete software system: start here

source.text: The complete software system: start here
Before this lesson: None

CV connection. Your CV connects full-stack platforms, backend APIs, databases, AI services, cloud deployment and integrations. This lesson supplies the vocabulary that connects those areas. [CV-1, CV-2]
Understand the basic pieces

Software is a set of instructions that a computer executes. An application is software built for a useful task, such as managing customer records. A system is the application plus the other components it needs: databases, networks, external services and people operating it.

Frontend means the part a user interacts with, usually in a browser. In your CV, React dashboards are frontends. Backend means the server-side code that validates requests, applies rules and accesses data. A database stores structured information so the application can find and change it later. A full-stack engineer works across frontend and backend; that does not mean one person must be equally expert in every tool.

Client and server describe roles in a conversation. A client asks; a server responds. A browser is a client of your API. Your API becomes a client when it calls OpenAI. A request is the message asking for something. A response contains the result or an error. An API, or application programming interface, is the agreed way one piece of software uses another.

Runtime is the environment executing a program: Python executes Python code; Node.js executes JavaScript outside a browser. A library is reusable code you call. A framework supplies an application structure and calls your code at defined points. A dependency is a package or service your application relies on. A process is a running program; a thread is an execution path inside a process.

JSON is a text format for exchanging objects, arrays, strings, numbers, booleans and null. An object contains named properties. JSON is not the same as a Python dictionary, although they can represent similar information. Serialization turns an in-memory value into a transferable representation; deserialization reads it back.
Follow one request, without skipping steps
Imagine a One System user asks, "Show this month's reporting totals." The following is a teaching example, not a reconstruction of your deployed code.

1. The browser sends a request to a backend endpoint, such as /reports/summary. 2. The backend checks who the user is and whether the requested report is allowed. 3. It asks PostgreSQL for the permitted records and computes the result. 4. It returns JSON such as {"report_count": 12}. 5. React reads the result and displays 12. If an AI assistant is involved, it can explain the authorized result; it does not become the source of truth for the number.

Production is the environment serving real users. Development is where changes are built. Staging is a production-like environment for testing before release. A feature working on your laptop is not by itself a production deployment.

Latency is how long one operation takes. Throughput is how many operations finish per unit of time. Concurrency is how many operations are in progress together. A system can have high throughput and still give some users slow responses.
Why not put everything in the frontend?

The browser is controlled by the user. Hiding a button does not prevent someone from calling the API directly. Secrets, authorization decisions and authoritative data changes belong on trusted server-side paths. Frontend validation improves usability; backend validation enforces rules.

Interview bridge: "I connect the UI, API, database and AI layer, but keep responsibilities clear. The database holds business facts, the backend enforces permissions, and the model helps interpret or generate content within those boundaries."
Memory cue: UI shows. API coordinates. Database remembers. Model assists. Backend authorizes.
Practice before reading the answers
E01.1 - Recall. Explain client, server, API and database in one sentence each.
E01.2 - Trace. A user changes a customer's status from New to Contacted. Name the components involved, in order.
E01.3 - Diagnose. A hidden admin button is the only protection around a delete endpoint. What is wrong?
Check your answers

E01.1: A client initiates a request; a server handles it; an API defines how software interacts; a database stores and retrieves data. A component can be a client in one interaction and a server in another.

E01.2: Browser form -> authenticated API -> permission and input checks -> database update -> response -> UI refresh. A background event or notification may follow, but it is not needed to understand the basic write path.
E01.3: A user can bypass the screen and send a request directly. The backend must verify authorization on the delete operation and on the specific target record.
Technical reading: [PY], [HTTP].

definitions.definition: It is a set of instructions that a computer executes to perform tasks.
definitions.example: A Python script that totals completed calls is software.
definitions.note: Software is the instructions, not the physical computer running them.

definitions.definition: An application is software built for a useful task or a related set of user tasks.
definitions.example: A customer-management application lets a team add contacts, update statuses and search records.
definitions.note: Every application is software, but software also includes tools that are not end-user applications.

definitions.definition: A system is the application plus the components it relies on, such as databases, networks, external services and people operating it.
definitions.example: A reporting system can include a React screen, a Flask API, PostgreSQL, scheduled jobs and its operators.
definitions.note: A working screen alone is not the complete system.

definitions.definition: The frontend is the part of an application that the user interacts with, often in a browser.
definitions.example: A table with a search box and an Edit button is frontend functionality.
definitions.note: Hiding a button does not prevent someone from calling the backend directly.

definitions.definition: The backend is server-side code that validates requests, applies business rules, enforces access permissions and works with data or other services.
definitions.example: When a user changes a contact's status, the backend checks permission and saves the change.
definitions.note: The backend must enforce rules even when the frontend already checks them.

definitions.definition: A database is an organized store of data that software can query and change.
definitions.example: PostgreSQL stores customer records so they remain available after a browser closes.
definitions.note: A database stores business facts; an AI-generated answer is not a replacement for those facts.

definitions.definition: Full-stack engineering involves working across the frontend and backend of an application.
definitions.example: An engineer builds a report API and the React page that displays its results.
definitions.note: Full-stack does not mean equally deep expertise in every technology.

definitions.definition: A client is a program or component that initiates a request to another component.
definitions.example: A browser is a client when it requests a report from your API.
definitions.note: Your backend becomes a client when it calls an external model API.

definitions.definition: A server is a program or machine that receives requests and provides responses or services.
definitions.example: A running Flask service receives GET /reports and returns report data.
definitions.note: Client and server are roles in an interaction, not permanent labels for every component.

definitions.definition: A request is a message asking another component to perform an operation or return information.
definitions.example: The browser asks the API to return the completed calls for October.
definitions.note: A request can fail or be denied; asking does not imply permission.

definitions.definition: A response is the result, status or error sent back after a request.
definitions.example: The API returns {"completed_calls":40} or a forbidden-access error.
definitions.note: A response should distinguish a genuine empty result from a failure.

definitions.definition: An API is an agreed interface through which one piece of software uses another's functionality or data.
definitions.example: A reporting API defines how to request a date range and how its totals are returned.
definitions.note: An API is the interface or contract; the backend is the code implementing it.

definitions.definition: A runtime is the execution environment that runs a program and provides facilities it needs.
definitions.example: Node.js runs JavaScript on a server; a Python interpreter runs a Python script.
definitions.note: A runtime is not the same thing as a programming language.

definitions.definition: A library is reusable code that your program calls to perform particular tasks.
definitions.example: Your code calls a Pandas function to read a CSV file.
definitions.note: You decide when to call library functionality.

definitions.definition: A framework supplies an application structure and invokes your code at defined extension points.
definitions.example: FastAPI calls your endpoint function when a matching HTTP request arrives.
definitions.note: The library/framework distinction is useful, but real products can combine both roles.

definitions.definition: A dependency is a package, service or resource that your software needs in order to work.
definitions.example: A backend may depend on its database driver, PostgreSQL and an external AI provider.
definitions.note: A dependency failing or changing can affect your application.

definitions.definition: A process is a running instance of a program with its own execution context and memory resources.
definitions.example: Starting two API worker processes creates two running instances of the backend.
definitions.note: A variable in one process is not automatically shared with another.

definitions.definition: A thread is an execution path inside a process; threads in that process share memory resources.
definitions.example: A server can use a thread to perform a blocking file operation.
definitions.note: Shared memory can introduce race conditions; threads are not automatically safe parallelism.

definitions.definition: JSON is a text format for exchanging objects, arrays, strings, numbers, booleans and null.
definitions.example: {"name":"Arslan","active":true} is JSON representing two named values.
definitions.note: JSON is text; a Python dictionary is an in-memory Python object.

definitions.definition: An object groups named properties or attributes into one value; the exact behavior depends on the language or format.
definitions.example: In JSON, {"status":"new","count":3} is an object with status and count properties.
definitions.note: A JSON object does not contain Python methods or arbitrary Python types.

definitions.definition: Serialization converts an in-memory value into a representation that can be stored or transmitted.
definitions.example: Converting a Python dictionary to JSON text before sending an HTTP response is serialization.
definitions.note: Not every in-memory value has an automatic or lossless JSON representation.

definitions.definition: Deserialization reads a stored or transmitted representation and creates corresponding in-memory values.
definitions.example: Parsing JSON text from an API creates an object that the application can inspect.
definitions.note: Parsing successfully does not prove the data is valid or authorized.

definitions.definition: The development environment is where engineers build and change software.
definitions.example: You run a local API with dummy records while implementing a new endpoint.
definitions.note: A feature working here has not necessarily been tested under production conditions.

definitions.definition: Staging is a testing environment intended to resemble production before a release reaches real users.
definitions.example: The team tests a new report against representative, safely handled data in staging.
definitions.note: Differences in data volume or configuration can still hide production problems.

definitions.definition: Production is the environment serving real users and real business operations.
definitions.example: Employees use the deployed reporting system for their daily work.
definitions.note: A demo on a laptop is not by itself a production deployment.

definitions.definition: Latency is the time one operation takes, measured between clearly defined start and end points.
definitions.example: A report request that starts at 10:00:00 and completes 300 milliseconds later has 300 ms latency.
definitions.note: Specify whether you mean server processing time or the user's full waiting time.

definitions.definition: Throughput is how many operations a system completes per unit of time.
definitions.example: A worker finishing 600 records in one minute achieves 10 records per second on average.
definitions.note: High throughput does not guarantee low latency for every individual request.

definitions.definition: Concurrency is the number of operations in progress together, or their overlapping progress over time.
definitions.example: An API can have 30 model requests waiting for network responses at the same time.
definitions.note: Concurrent work does not necessarily execute on 30 CPU cores.

definitions.definition: A business rule is a domain-specific constraint or decision the application must enforce.
definitions.example: Only a manager may approve a report for their own department.
definitions.note: Valid JSON can still violate a business rule.

definitions.definition: Validation checks whether data satisfies declared structural or business requirements.
definitions.example: Rejecting a negative call duration is validation.
definitions.note: Validation and authorization answer different questions: is it valid, and is this user allowed?

definitions.definition: A source of truth is the authoritative place used to determine a particular fact.
definitions.example: Use the approved reporting query for revenue totals instead of asking an LLM to guess them.
definitions.note: Different systems may own different facts; ownership should be explicit.

lessons.title: Python: values, collections, functions and safe code

source.text: Python: values, collections, functions and safe code
Before this lesson: Lesson 1
CV connection. Python appears throughout your FastAPI/Flask services, data pipelines, ML work and Skills Stack packaging tools. [CV-1, CV-2]
The vocabulary of a small Python program

A variable is a name referring to a value. Common types include int for integers, float for approximate decimal numbers, str for text, and bool for true/false. None represents the absence of a value. A condition selects a branch; a loop repeats work.

A list is an ordered collection, such as a batch of call records. A tuple is an ordered collection whose elements cannot be reassigned. A dictionary maps keys to values, such as a customer ID to a customer record. A set stores distinct values and is useful for membership checks. Lists and dictionaries are mutable: you can change their contents after creating them.

A function packages a reusable operation. A parameter is a name in the definition; an argument is a value supplied by a caller. A return value is the result sent back. A type hint documents expected types and helps tools check code; ordinary Python does not enforce every hint at runtime.

An exception signals that an operation cannot continue normally. Catch expected exceptions where you can handle them; do not catch everything and pretend success. A module is an importable Python file; a package groups modules. A virtual environment gives a project its own installed dependencies.

A class defines a kind of object with data and behavior. An instance is a concrete object of that class. For example, a ReportService class could coordinate report operations. You do not need a class for every short function. A context manager, used with with, manages setup and cleanup, such as closing a file.
Worked example: deduplicate without losing order
Save this as dedupe.py and run python dedupe.py. It uses only Python's standard library.
sample = [" A@EXAMPLE.COM ", "b@example.com", "a@example.com"] print(unique_emails(sample)) # ['a@example.com', 'b@example.com']

strip removes surrounding whitespace; lower applies lowercase; the set remembers values already encountered; the list preserves first-occurrence order. This is a simplified normalization policy, not full email-address validation. A real product must decide whether lowercasing the entire address is acceptable for its requirements.

Complexity describes how work grows with input size. This algorithm is approximately O(n) expected time because it visits n values once and set lookups are expected O(1). It uses O(n) extra space. A nested scan through all previous values can become O(n squared). Constants and actual input sizes still matter.
Common mistakes and choices
Why a set and a list? A set helps check membership efficiently; the list preserves an intentional output order. Using only a set loses the explicit ordering contract.

Why not a global mutable list? Shared state can leak between users or requests and is not automatically synchronized across server processes. Keep request data local; persist shared business state in an appropriate store.

What about generators? A generator yields values one at a time instead of building the whole result first. It can reduce memory for streamed data, but operations such as complete sorting still need broader access to the data.
Memory cue: List orders; dictionary maps; set deduplicates; function organizes; exception reports failure.
Practice before reading the answers
E02.1 - Predict. What does unique_emails(["", " x@test.com ", "X@test.com"]) return under this example's policy?
E02.2 - Modify. The business now wants duplicates preserved. Which part of the logic changes?
E02.3 - Explain. Why does annotating age: int not prove that an HTTP request contains an integer?
Check your answers
E02.1: ['x@test.com']. The empty value is skipped; the two other strings normalize to the same value.
E02.2: Remove the membership check and seen set, then append every nonempty normalized value. Duplicate removal is a business rule, not universally correct cleanup.
E02.3: HTTP input arrives from outside your program. Type hints do not inspect that input automatically. Parse and validate the actual value, for example through a runtime schema such as Pydantic.
Technical reading: [PY].

exercises.answer: Remove the membership check and seen set, then append every nonempty normalized value. Duplicate removal is a business rule, not universally correct cleanup.

definitions.definition: Python is a general-purpose programming language used in backend services, automation, data analysis and machine learning.
definitions.example: A Python function can validate uploaded records before saving them.
definitions.note: The language alone does not provide deployment, permissions or production reliability.

definitions.definition: A variable is a name that refers to a value.
definitions.example: count = 3 makes count refer to the integer 3.
definitions.note: Assigning a name to a mutable object does not automatically copy that object.

definitions.definition: An integer represents a whole number without a fractional part.
definitions.example: completed_calls = 40 stores a whole-number count.
definitions.note: Use an appropriate numeric type rather than text for arithmetic.

definitions.definition: A float represents an approximate real number using floating-point arithmetic.
definitions.example: duration = 1.25 can represent a measured number of seconds.
definitions.note: Some decimal fractions cannot be represented exactly; money may need decimal arithmetic or integer minor units.

definitions.definition: A string is a sequence of text characters.
definitions.example: email = "a@example.com" stores text rather than an email object with built-in validation.
definitions.note: A string that looks like a date is still text until interpreted or converted.

definitions.definition: A Boolean represents one of two logical values: True or False.
definitions.example: is_completed = True can mark a finished job.
definitions.note: The string "False" is nonempty text, not the Boolean False.

definitions.definition: None is Python's value for the absence of a value or result.
definitions.example: A lookup returns None when no matching record is found.
definitions.note: None is different from zero, an empty string and False.

definitions.definition: A condition is an expression whose result determines which branch of code executes.
definitions.example: if count > 0: runs its block only when count is positive.
definitions.note: Check the intended condition instead of relying on accidental truthiness.

definitions.definition: A loop repeats an operation over items or while a condition remains true.
definitions.example: for email in emails: processes each supplied email.
definitions.note: A loop needs a finite collection or a reliable stopping condition.

definitions.definition: A list is an ordered, mutable collection of items in Python.
definitions.example: ["new", "contacted", "closed"] preserves those values in that order.
definitions.note: Lists allow duplicate values.

definitions.definition: A tuple is an ordered collection whose item references cannot be reassigned after creation.
definitions.example: (10, 20) can represent a fixed coordinate pair.
definitions.note: A mutable object inside a tuple can still change internally.

definitions.definition: A dictionary maps unique, hashable keys to associated values.
definitions.example: {"customer_id":42,"status":"new"} lets you retrieve the status by its key.
definitions.note: A dictionary is useful for lookup, not a replacement for persistent database storage.

definitions.definition: A set stores distinct, hashable values and supports membership tests.
definitions.example: {"a@example.com","b@example.com"} can track emails already encountered.
definitions.note: Do not depend on set iteration for a meaningful display order.

definitions.definition: Mutability means an object's contents can change after the object is created.
definitions.example: Appending an item changes an existing list; a string operation produces a new string.
definitions.note: Two names referring to the same list observe changes to that shared list.

definitions.definition: A function is a reusable block of code that accepts inputs and may return a result.
definitions.example: def double(x): return x * 2 defines a reusable calculation.
definitions.note: Prefer explicit inputs and outputs over hidden changes to shared state.

definitions.definition: A parameter is the name used in a function definition for an expected input.
definitions.example: In def double(x), x is a parameter.
definitions.note: A parameter is the placeholder; an argument is the supplied value.

definitions.definition: An argument is a value passed to a function when it is called.
definitions.example: In double(4), the value 4 is the argument.
definitions.note: The same function can receive different arguments on different calls.

definitions.definition: A return value is the result a function sends back to its caller.
definitions.example: double(4) returns 8, which another calculation can use.
definitions.note: Printing a value is not the same as returning it.

definitions.definition: A type hint declares an expected type for tools and readers without automatically enforcing all such declarations at runtime.
definitions.example: def total(values: list[int]) -> int documents the expected input and output.
definitions.note: Untrusted HTTP input still needs runtime validation.

definitions.definition: An exception signals an abnormal condition that interrupts normal execution unless it is handled.
definitions.example: Converting "hello" to an integer raises a ValueError.
definitions.note: Do not catch every exception and silently return a fake success.

definitions.definition: A module is an importable unit of Python code, commonly a .py file.
definitions.example: helpers.py can define a function imported by app.py.
definitions.note: Importing a module may execute its top-level code.

definitions.definition: A package organizes related Python modules under an importable namespace.
definitions.example: A reporting package can contain database, calculations and export modules.
definitions.note: An installed distribution and an import package are related but not always named identically.

definitions.definition: A virtual environment gives a Python project its own interpreter environment and installed dependencies.
definitions.example: Two projects can use separate environments with different library versions.
definitions.note: It does not isolate a program from the operating system like a security sandbox.

definitions.definition: A class defines a type of object, including its data and behavior.
definitions.example: A ReportService class can define how report queries are coordinated.
definitions.note: A small stateless task may only need a function, not a class.

definitions.definition: An instance is a concrete object created from a class.
definitions.example: service = ReportService() creates an instance you can call.
definitions.note: A class is the definition; instances are the objects created from it.

definitions.definition: A context manager handles entry and cleanup around a block of code, commonly through with.
definitions.example: with open("notes.txt") as f: closes the file after the block finishes.
definitions.note: Cleanup should still happen when an exception leaves the block.

definitions.definition: A generator produces values incrementally instead of building a complete result collection first.
definitions.example: A CSV reader can yield one cleaned row at a time.
definitions.note: Streaming reduces some memory use, but collecting all yielded items removes that advantage.

definitions.definition: Deduplication removes repeated occurrences according to an explicitly chosen identity rule.
definitions.example: Keep the first occurrence of each normalized email while preserving input order.
definitions.note: Two identical-looking event rows may represent two real events and should not automatically be removed.

definitions.definition: Input normalization transforms equivalent forms into a consistent representation under a chosen policy.
definitions.example: Strip surrounding spaces from an email before comparing it with existing values.
definitions.note: Lowercasing an entire email address is a policy choice, not universal email validation.

definitions.definition: Algorithmic complexity describes how an algorithm's resource use grows as input size grows.
definitions.example: Processing each of n records once is typically linear work, written O(n).
definitions.note: Big O describes growth, not the exact time on a particular computer.

definitions.definition: Expected constant-time lookup means average lookup work does not grow proportionally with the number of stored items under the data structure's assumptions.
definitions.example: A set can efficiently check whether an email has already been seen.
definitions.note: Expected performance is not a worst-case guarantee for every input.

definitions.definition: O(n) space means extra memory can grow in proportion to the number of input items.
definitions.example: Keeping every unique input in a set can require storage proportional to n.
definitions.note: A fast algorithm can still use substantial memory.

lessons.title: Asyncio, concurrency and background work

source.text: Asyncio, concurrency and background work
Before this lesson: Lessons 1-2
CV connection. Your outbound calling backend is asynchronous FastAPI with WebSocket audio streaming; asyncio is listed explicitly. [CV-1]
Start with waiting versus calculating

I/O, or input/output, means communicating with something outside the current computation: a network service, disk or database. I/O-bound work spends much of its time waiting. CPU-bound work spends much of its time calculating. Waiting for a model API is usually I/O-bound in your application; running a large local model is compute-heavy.

Synchronous code ordinarily waits for an operation before moving on. Asynchronous code can give other tasks a chance to run while an operation is waiting. Concurrency is overlapping progress. Parallelism is genuinely simultaneous execution on separate processing resources. Async is not another word for parallelism.

In Python, async def defines a coroutine function. Calling it creates a coroutine object; it does not complete the work immediately. await suspends the current coroutine while waiting on an awaitable result. The event loop schedules runnable tasks. A task wraps a coroutine so the event loop can manage it.

A timeout limits waiting time. Cancellation requests that unfinished work stop. A semaphore limits how many operations enter a section at once. Backpressure means slowing or rejecting incoming work when consumers cannot keep up, rather than allowing an unbounded queue or memory buffer.
Worked example: overlap two independent waits
Save as async_demo.py. The delays imitate network waiting; no network service is contacted.

import asyncio
   import time

async def fetch_report(name: str) -> str:
       await asyncio.sleep(0.2)
       return f"{name}: ready"

async def main() -> None:
       start = time.perf_counter()
       results = await asyncio.gather(
           fetch_report("sales"), fetch_report("calls")
       )
       print(results)
       print(round(time.perf_counter() - start, 2))
asyncio.run(main())

Both waits can overlap, so elapsed time is about 0.2 seconds plus overhead, rather than about 0.4 seconds. gather returns results in the supplied order. This example does not claim all async operations finish faster or succeed together.

Replacing await asyncio.sleep(...) with time.sleep(...) blocks that event-loop thread. Likewise, a synchronous HTTP library or expensive Python loop inside async def can block other requests. Calling a function async does not transform its internal work into nonblocking operations.
Choose the right execution location

For concurrent external API calls, use an asynchronous client, explicit deadlines and a concurrency limit. For blocking I/O that cannot be changed, a carefully bounded thread pool may help. For CPU-heavy Python work, consider processes, specialized libraries or a separate worker service. Traditional CPython's GIL, or Global Interpreter Lock, limits concurrent Python bytecode execution by threads within one interpreter; details depend on the Python build and native libraries.

A background job runs separately from the request-response path. A durable queue is appropriate when work must survive application restart. Creating an in-memory async task is not equivalent to a durable queue. In the calling system, audio handling is time- sensitive, while a CRM summary can usually be queued separately.

Why not launch 10,000 calls at once? Unlimited concurrency can exhaust connections, memory or provider quotas. More concurrency is useful only while dependencies have capacity. Choose limits from measurement, not just the number of records.
Memory cue: Async shares waiting time; workers isolate heavy work; queues preserve work.
Practice before reading the answers
E03.1 - Classify. Waiting on OpenAI, calculating embeddings locally, and sending a HubSpot update: which are generally I/O-bound from the caller's perspective?
E03.2 - Debug. An async def endpoint uses time.sleep(5). What would you change for a deliberate delay?
E03.3 - Design. An HTTP request must trigger a report that takes two minutes and survives a restart. Is asyncio.create_task enough?
Check your answers

E03.1: Remote OpenAI and HubSpot calls are generally I/O-bound in the calling process. Local embedding inference consumes compute, possibly GPU rather than CPU. Remote embedding APIs again look like I/O to your caller.
E03.2: Use await asyncio.sleep(5) for a nonblocking timer. This fixes the artificial delay, not unrelated blocking libraries elsewhere in the endpoint.
E03.3: No. Persist a job through a durable queue, return a job ID, and expose status. Make the worker safe to retry. An in-memory task can disappear with its process.
Technical reading: [ASYNC], [FASTASYNC], [NODE].

definitions.definition: I/O is communication with something outside the current calculation, such as a file, database or network service.
definitions.example: Waiting for an HTTP response from a model provider is network I/O.
definitions.note: Waiting time and calculation time need different optimization strategies.

definitions.definition: I/O-bound work spends much of its time waiting for external data or operations.
definitions.example: A backend waiting for five independent API responses is usually I/O-bound.
definitions.note: Async can improve overlapping waits; it does not remove the remote service's latency.

definitions.definition: CPU-bound work spends much of its time computing rather than waiting.
definitions.example: Calculating a large transformation in pure Python can keep a CPU busy.
definitions.note: Adding async keywords does not make that calculation run on another processor.

definitions.definition: Synchronous execution follows a call until it finishes before continuing that execution path.
definitions.example: A blocking HTTP call holds its thread until the response arrives.
definitions.note: Other threads or processes may still run; synchronous does not mean the whole machine stops.

definitions.definition: Asynchronous execution allows a task to suspend while waiting so other work can progress.
definitions.example: An async backend serves other connections while one request awaits a model response.
definitions.note: It only helps when the awaited operations cooperate with the execution model.

definitions.definition: Parallelism is simultaneous execution on separate processing resources.
definitions.example: Two processes can compute separate batches on different CPU cores.
definitions.note: Concurrency is overlapping progress; parallelism is actual simultaneous computation.

definitions.definition: A coroutine is a computation that can suspend and resume; in Python, calling async def creates a coroutine object.
definitions.example: Calling fetch_report() returns a coroutine that must be awaited or scheduled.
definitions.note: Creating the object does not mean the requested work has already completed.

definitions.definition: await suspends the current coroutine until an awaitable completes and then provides its result.
definitions.example: report = await fetch_report() waits without necessarily blocking the entire event-loop thread.
definitions.note: Awaiting a nonblocking function is different from calling blocking code inside async def.

definitions.definition: An event loop schedules runnable tasks and responds to events or completed I/O.
definitions.example: While task A waits on a socket, the loop runs task B.
definitions.note: A long blocking calculation on the event-loop thread delays unrelated tasks.

definitions.definition: A task is a scheduled coroutine managed by the event loop.
definitions.example: asyncio.create_task(fetch_report()) schedules the coroutine to make progress.
definitions.note: Untracked tasks can hide exceptions or outlive the request that created them.

definitions.definition: asyncio is Python's standard-library framework for asynchronous I/O, tasks, synchronization and related control flow.
definitions.example: asyncio.gather can wait for several independent async operations.
definitions.note: It is not a durable background-job system.

definitions.definition: A timeout sets a maximum waiting duration for an operation or group of operations.
definitions.example: Stop waiting for a report provider after a defined deadline and return an honest failure.
definitions.note: A local timeout does not prove the remote system did not perform an action.

definitions.definition: Cancellation requests that unfinished work stop and release resources safely.
definitions.example: When a user disconnects, stop generating an answer that is no longer needed.
definitions.note: Cancellation is cooperative and does not automatically undo completed side effects.

definitions.definition: A semaphore limits how many tasks may enter a protected section at once.
definitions.example: Allow at most five simultaneous requests to an external provider.
definitions.note: Creating millions of waiting tasks still uses memory even with a semaphore.

definitions.definition: Backpressure slows, bounds or rejects incoming work when downstream processing cannot keep up.
definitions.example: Pause reading a stream when its bounded processing buffer is full.
definitions.note: An unlimited queue hides overload until latency or memory becomes unacceptable.

definitions.definition: A blocking call occupies its execution thread while waiting or computing.
definitions.example: time.sleep inside an async endpoint blocks the event-loop thread.
definitions.note: Use suitable async I/O, a thread for appropriate blocking I/O, or a process for suitable CPU work.

definitions.definition: A thread pool reuses a bounded number of threads to run delegated tasks.
definitions.example: A legacy blocking file operation runs in a worker thread instead of the event loop.
definitions.note: A thread pool can saturate; adding threads does not fix unlimited load.

definitions.definition: Multiprocessing runs work in separate processes with separate memory spaces.
definitions.example: Independent CPU-heavy batches can be assigned to worker processes.
definitions.note: Moving data between processes introduces serialization and coordination costs.

definitions.definition: In traditional CPython builds, the GIL limits simultaneous execution of Python bytecode by threads in one interpreter.
definitions.example: Two pure-Python CPU threads may not double calculation throughput in such a build.
definitions.note: Behavior depends on the Python build, native libraries and workload; free-threaded builds differ.

definitions.definition: A background job is work executed outside the immediate request path, often by a separate worker.
definitions.example: An import continues through a durable queue after the API returns a job ID.
definitions.note: An in-process background task may be lost if the process dies.

definitions.definition: Bounded concurrency limits the number of operations active together to a controlled amount.
definitions.example: Process an import in batches of 20 API calls rather than sending all 50,000 at once.
definitions.note: The right limit depends on resources, quotas and measured response behavior.

lessons.title: JavaScript, TypeScript and Node.js

source.text: JavaScript, TypeScript and Node.js
Before this lesson: Lessons 1-3
CV connection. Your CV lists JavaScript, TypeScript and Node.js; TableOS is a TypeScript monorepo with a Fastify backend. [CV-1, CV-2]
Three names, three different roles

JavaScript is the programming language. It runs in browsers and in other environments. Node.js is a runtime that lets JavaScript execute on servers and provides facilities such as networking and file access. TypeScript adds a static type system to JavaScript. TypeScript code is transformed into JavaScript for execution in typical toolchains; types are not automatic runtime validation.

An object groups named values; an array is an ordered collection. const prevents reassigning a variable binding, but does not freeze every property of an object. let allows reassignment. Strict equality, ===, avoids many implicit conversions performed by ==.

A Promise represents a future completion or failure. async functions return promises; await pauses that function until the awaited value settles. The Node.js event loop supports many concurrent I/O operations, but a long synchronous calculation can prevent it from serving other work promptly.

A type alias names a type, including unions. An interface describes an object contract. A union permits one of several alternatives. A generic expresses a reusable relationship between types. Narrowing uses checks to determine which alternative is currently present. unknown requires checks before use; any bypasses much of the safety TypeScript offers.
Worked example: represent success and failure clearly
This is a TypeScript teaching snippet, intended for a TypeScript project or playground.
type Result<T> = | { ok: true; value: T } | { ok: false; error: string };

Result<T> means the successful value has type T. The ok field distinguishes the two shapes. The caller checks ok before reading value; that check is narrowing. Crucially, typeof and Number.isInteger are real runtime checks. Merely casting a value using as number would not validate it.
Why TypeScript for TableOS rather than Python everywhere?

A defensible explanation is shared language and contracts across a substantial frontend/ backend product, together with a suitable Node.js ecosystem. That is a design rationale to confirm against your actual decision. It does not imply TypeScript is inherently more scalable than Python. Python remains attractive for ML libraries and AI-focused services.

Why not plain JavaScript? TypeScript can catch incompatible interfaces during development and support large refactors. It adds build and typing overhead, so its value is strongest when the system is large enough for those checks to matter.

Why not trust a typed API response? A network response may violate the assumed type because of bugs, outdated versions or malicious input. Validate at trust boundaries, then use static typing inside the program.

Why not do a large CSV transformation on the event loop? CPU-heavy synchronous work delays unrelated requests. Stream bounded batches or use suitable workers. Do not confuse a promise with automatic offloading to another CPU.
Memory cue: JavaScript is the language; Node is the runtime; TypeScript checks contracts before runtime.
Practice before reading the answers
E04.1 - Recall. Is TypeScript a replacement for backend input validation? Explain.
E04.2 - Predict. What does parseCount("12") return? What about parseCount(-1)?
E04.3 - Compare. A teammate says, "Node handles I/O well, so every operation can run in one server process." What is missing?
Check your answers
E04.1: No. TypeScript verifies code under its declared assumptions. Incoming bytes still require runtime checks. Static types disappear from ordinary runtime data.
E04.2: The string fails the integer check; -1 fails the nonnegative rule. The error messages explain different failures. Automatic coercion would require an explicit policy.
E04.3: CPU work, memory limits, process failure, database capacity and horizontal scaling still matter. An event loop is a concurrency mechanism, not unlimited compute or reliability.
Technical reading: [TS], [NODE].

exercises.answer: The string fails the integer check; -1 fails the nonnegative rule. The error messages explain different failures. Automatic coercion would require an explicit policy.

exercises.answer: CPU work, memory limits, process failure, database capacity and horizontal scaling still matter. An event loop is a concurrency mechanism, not unlimited compute or reliability.

definitions.definition: JavaScript is a programming language used in browsers and other runtimes such as Node.js.
definitions.example: It can handle a button click or implement a server-side API.
definitions.note: JavaScript is the language; Node.js is one environment that runs it.

definitions.definition: TypeScript adds static type checking and type syntax to JavaScript to catch many mistakes before execution.
definitions.example: A type checker can reject passing a string to a function declared to accept a number.
definitions.note: Type annotations do not validate incoming JSON at runtime.

definitions.definition: Node.js is a JavaScript runtime with facilities for server-side networking, files and other system operations.
definitions.example: A Fastify application runs on Node.js and responds to HTTP requests.
definitions.note: Node.js is not itself a web framework.

definitions.definition: An array is an ordered, indexed collection of values in JavaScript.
definitions.example: ["new", "done"] stores two statuses that can be accessed by position.
definitions.note: Arrays can contain duplicates; TypeScript can constrain element types during development.

definitions.definition: const declares a binding that cannot be reassigned after initialization.
definitions.example: const user = {name:"Ali"} prevents assigning a different object to user.
definitions.note: It does not prevent changing user.name unless further controls are used.

definitions.definition: let declares a block-scoped binding that may be reassigned.
definitions.example: let count = 0; count = count + 1; changes the referenced value.
definitions.note: Prefer the narrowest useful scope instead of shared mutable state.

definitions.definition: Strict equality compares values without the broad type coercions performed by ==.
definitions.example: 3 === "3" evaluates to false.
definitions.note: Object equality compares identity, not a deep comparison of every property.

definitions.definition: A Promise represents the eventual success or failure of an asynchronous operation.
definitions.example: fetch(url) returns a Promise for a response.
definitions.note: A Promise does not automatically move CPU-heavy work to a separate thread.

definitions.definition: An async JavaScript function always returns a Promise and allows await inside its body.
definitions.example: An async loadReport function can await a network request and return its parsed result.
definitions.note: Code before an awaited suspension still executes on the current execution path.

definitions.definition: A type alias gives a name to a TypeScript type expression.
definitions.example: type Status = "new" | "done" names a union of two allowed strings.
definitions.note: A type alias does not create a runtime validator.

definitions.definition: An interface describes the required shape of an object in TypeScript.
definitions.example: interface User { id: number } describes an object with a numeric id.
definitions.note: Real data can violate that assumed shape unless it is checked at the boundary.

definitions.definition: A union allows a value to be one of several declared types or alternatives.
definitions.example: A result may be {ok:true,value:7} or {ok:false,error:"Invalid"}.
definitions.note: Check which alternative you have before accessing fields unique to it.

definitions.definition: A generic expresses a reusable type relationship using a type parameter.
definitions.example: Result<T> can represent a successful number or string while retaining the correct value type.
definitions.note: Generics describe type relationships, not automatic runtime conversions.

definitions.definition: Narrowing uses checks to refine the possible type of a value within a code branch.
definitions.example: After typeof value === "number", TypeScript can treat value as numeric in that branch.
definitions.note: A type assertion is not the same thing as a real check.

definitions.definition: unknown is a TypeScript type for a value whose type must be checked before most specific operations.
definitions.example: Treat parsed external input as unknown, then validate it before reading fields.
definitions.note: It preserves more safety than any.

definitions.definition: any tells TypeScript to allow many operations without normal type checking for that value.
definitions.example: Calling a nonexistent method may compile when a value is typed any.
definitions.note: Use it deliberately; it can hide errors instead of solving them.

definitions.definition: A type assertion tells the TypeScript checker to treat a value as a chosen type.
definitions.example: value as number changes the checker's view of value.
definitions.note: It does not convert "abc" into a number or prove the value is valid.

definitions.definition: Runtime validation checks real values while the program runs.
definitions.example: Number.isInteger(value) verifies that a supplied numeric value is an integer.
definitions.note: Static type checking and runtime validation protect different stages.

definitions.definition: A discriminated union distinguishes object alternatives using a shared field with different literal values.
definitions.example: Check result.ok before choosing result.value or result.error.
definitions.note: Use the discriminating field rather than guessing which properties exist.

definitions.definition: A trust boundary is a point where data moves between components with different trust assumptions.
definitions.example: HTTP input crosses from a user-controlled browser into the backend.
definitions.note: Validate and authorize at the boundary instead of assuming declared types make it trusted.

lessons.title: APIs, REST, OpenAPI, FastAPI, Flask and Fastify

source.text: APIs, REST, OpenAPI, FastAPI, Flask and Fastify
Before this lesson: Lessons 1-4
CV connection. FastAPI, Flask, Pydantic, Fastify, REST APIs and OpenAPI are all named in your CV. One System contains 120+ REST endpoints. [CV-1, CV-2]
Learn the request vocabulary first

HTTP is a request-response protocol used on the web. A request has a method describing the operation, a path identifying the target, headers carrying metadata, and sometimes a body carrying data. An endpoint is a particular API operation, usually a method and path together.

Common methods are GET to read, POST to submit or create, PUT to replace a representation, PATCH to partially modify, and DELETE to remove. REST is an architectural style based on resources, representations and constraints such as stateless interactions; not every JSON-over-HTTP API implements every REST constraint.

A status code communicates the result: 200 success, 201 created, 202 accepted for processing, 400 invalid request, 401 missing/invalid authentication, 403 forbidden, 404 not found, 409 conflict, 429 rate limited, and 500 server failure. Pagination divides a large result into pages. A cursor identifies where to continue; an offset skips a specified number of rows.

Validation checks whether input meets rules. Serialization produces the output format. OpenAPI is a machine-readable description of API operations, input/output schemas and authentication schemes. It is a contract format, not a server framework.
What each framework does

FastAPI is a Python web framework built around type annotations, runtime validation and an asynchronous server interface. Pydantic validates and constructs structured Python data using declared models. Flask is a lightweight Python web framework with an extensible ecosystem. Fastify is a Node.js web framework with schema-based validation/ serialization and a plugin model.

WSGI is a traditional Python web-server/application interface; ASGI accommodates asynchronous interactions, including long-lived connections. definitions.definition: HTTP is an application protocol for exchanging requests and responses on the web.
definitions.example: A browser sends a request and receives a status code, headers and a response body.
definitions.note: HTTP describes communication; your application defines its business rules.

definitions.definition: An HTTP method describes the intended kind of operation on a target resource.
definitions.example: GET reads a report; POST can submit a new job.
definitions.note: Methods have defined semantics that caches and clients may rely on.

definitions.definition: An endpoint is a particular API operation identified by its interface, commonly an HTTP method and path.
definitions.example: POST /questions and GET /questions are different operations on the same path.
definitions.note: A URL alone may not fully describe an operation.

definitions.definition: A header carries request or response metadata outside the body.
definitions.example: Content-Type: application/json tells the recipient how the body is represented.
definitions.note: Do not log sensitive authorization headers indiscriminately.

definitions.definition: A request body carries the main submitted data when the operation supports it.
definitions.example: A create-contact request can contain {"name":"Ali"}.
definitions.note: The server must validate the body rather than trust its declared format.

definitions.definition: REST is an architectural style based on resources, representations, stateless interactions and a uniform interface.
definitions.example: A client uses documented resource operations to read and update contacts.
definitions.note: Not every JSON-over-HTTP API implements every REST constraint.

definitions.definition: GET requests a representation of a resource and is intended to be safe and read-only in its semantics.
definitions.example: GET /reports/42 retrieves a report.
definitions.note: Do not use GET to trigger an intended destructive business change.

definitions.definition: POST submits data for processing according to the target resource's rules.
definitions.example: POST /imports submits a new import job.
definitions.note: Repeated POST requests may repeat effects unless the application handles idempotency.

definitions.definition: PUT creates or replaces the target resource's representation according to the API contract.
definitions.example: PUT /settings/profile sends the complete replacement profile representation.
definitions.note: A repeated identical PUT has idempotent intended semantics.

definitions.definition: PATCH applies a specified partial modification to a resource.
definitions.example: A patch changes only a customer's status.
definitions.note: PATCH is not inherently idempotent: incrementing a counter differs from setting it to 5.

definitions.definition: DELETE requests removal of the association represented by the target resource.
definitions.example: DELETE /contacts/42 removes that contact under the application's rules.
definitions.note: The final intended state can be idempotent even when later response codes differ.

definitions.definition: A status code is a numeric HTTP result indicator.
definitions.example: 201 means created; 202 means accepted for processing; 429 means rate limited.
definitions.note: 202 does not mean the background work is finished.

definitions.definition: 401 indicates missing or invalid authentication for a protected operation; 403 indicates that the request is forbidden.
definitions.example: A missing credential can yield 401; a signed-in viewer attempting an admin action can yield 403.
definitions.note: Applications may deliberately return 404 to avoid revealing a protected resource's existence.

definitions.definition: Pagination divides a large result into smaller, ordered portions.
definitions.example: Return 50 records and instructions for retrieving the next portion.
definitions.note: Define a stable ordering and maximum page size.

definitions.definition: Cursor pagination continues from an encoded position in an ordered result.
definitions.example: After the last seen timestamp and ID, request records beyond that position.
definitions.note: A cursor must be validated and should bind the relevant query context.

definitions.definition: Offset pagination skips a specified number of rows before returning a page.
definitions.example: LIMIT 20 OFFSET 40 asks for the third 20-row page.
definitions.note: Large offsets can be expensive, and concurrent changes can shift page contents.

definitions.definition: OpenAPI is a machine-readable specification format for HTTP API operations, schemas and security schemes.
definitions.example: A specification documents the fields accepted by POST /questions.
definitions.note: Documentation must stay consistent with implementation and tests.

definitions.definition: FastAPI is a Python web framework that uses type annotations, validation and an asynchronous server interface to build APIs.
definitions.example: An endpoint accepts a validated question model and returns a JSON answer.
definitions.note: Its async support does not make blocking dependencies nonblocking.

definitions.definition: Pydantic validates and constructs Python data structures from declared models and rules.
definitions.example: A Question model can require nonempty text and reject unexpected fields.
definitions.note: Schema validation does not establish that a user is authorized to access a record.

definitions.definition: Flask is a lightweight Python web framework with an extensible ecosystem.
definitions.example: A Flask route queries PostgreSQL and returns a report.
definitions.note: A working Flask service need not be rewritten merely because another framework is newer.

definitions.definition: Fastify is a Node.js web framework with schema-oriented validation, serialization and a plugin system.
definitions.example: A TypeScript API declares a JSON schema for a create-record request.
definitions.note: Fastify is a framework running on Node.js, not a database.

definitions.definition: WSGI is a traditional Python interface between web servers and applications.
definitions.example: A conventional Flask deployment handles requests through WSGI workers.
definitions.note: An async Flask view in a normal WSGI deployment still occupies a worker for that request.

definitions.definition: ASGI is an interface for Python applications that supports asynchronous and long-lived interactions.
definitions.example: An ASGI server hosts a FastAPI application with HTTP and WebSocket endpoints.
definitions.note: The interface enables concurrency patterns; application code must still use them correctly.

lessons.title: SQL, relational data and Kysely

source.text: SQL, relational data and Kysely
Before this lesson: Lessons 1, 4-5
CV connection. SQL, PostgreSQL and Kysely appear in your skills; reporting and relational platform work depend on these foundations. [CV-1, CV-2]
The database vocabulary

A relational database organizes data into tables and relationships. A row is one record; a column is one attribute. A schema describes structure and, in PostgreSQL, can also mean a named namespace containing objects. A primary key uniquely identifies a row. A foreign key requires a reference to an existing related row, subject to its constraint rules.

SQL, Structured Query Language, describes queries and changes. SELECT reads; INSERT creates; UPDATE changes; DELETE removes. WHERE filters rows. ORDER BY sorts. GROUP BY forms groups; an aggregate, such as COUNT or SUM, summarizes them. HAVING filters groups after aggregation.

A JOIN combines related rows. An inner join retains matches. A left join preserves all left- side rows and fills missing right-side values with NULL. NULL represents missing or unknown information; compare with IS NULL, not = NULL. A constraint enforces a rule, such as uniqueness or nonnegative amounts.

Normalization separates entities to avoid inconsistent duplication. Denormalization deliberately duplicates or precomputes data to simplify reads, but creates maintenance work. A migration is a versioned database-structure change. An upsert inserts a row or updates an existing conflict target.
Worked example: count calls per customer
Assume a small learning database with customers(id, name) and calls(id, customer_id, status).

SELECT c.id, c.name, COUNT(k.id) AS completed_calls
   FROM customers AS c
   LEFT JOIN calls AS k
     ON k.customer_id = c.id
    AND k.status = 'completed'
   GROUP BY c.id, c.name
   ORDER BY completed_calls DESC, c.id;

The filter is inside ON so customers with no completed calls remain in the result. COUNT(k.id) counts matching non-NULL call IDs. COUNT(*) would count the preserved left- join row and incorrectly give 1 for a customer with no matching calls. Moving the call- status condition into WHERE would remove those unmatched rows.

Kysely is a type-safe TypeScript SQL query builder. It helps you compose SQL while checking known table and column types. It is not a database engine and does not remove the need to understand joins, indexes or transactions. An ORM, object-relational mapper, offers a more object-oriented model of persistence; a query builder generally keeps SQL structure more visible. [KYSELY]
Transactions and trustworthy writes

A transaction groups operations into one unit of work. Atomicity means all-or-nothing. Consistency means database rules remain satisfied. Isolation specifies how concurrent transactions interact. Durability concerns committed changes surviving failures under the configured guarantees. Together these are ACID.

Example: updating a record and inserting its audit event should either both commit or both fail. A transaction does not automatically make a call to an unrelated external service atomic with that database update; Lesson 8 explains the outbox pattern.

Use parameterized queries for user-provided values. Parameters separate SQL structure from data. Dynamic column/table names still need safe allowlists or query- builder identifier handling. Never concatenate untrusted strings into executable SQL.
Choice and interview bridge

"I use relational constraints for business integrity, not only application checks. With Kysely I retain SQL-level control while benefiting from TypeScript contracts. I still inspect the generated query and execution plan when performance matters."
Memory cue: Rows represent things; keys identify/link them; joins combine; transactions protect changes.
Practice before reading the answers
E06.1: A customer has zero calls. Why can COUNT(*) return 1 after a left join?
E06.2: You update a record, then fail to write the audit entry. What prevents a partial database result?
E06.3: Does a query builder prove that a query is efficient or tenant-safe?
Check your answers
E06.1: The left join preserves one row for that customer, with NULL right-side values. Count a nonnullable right-side identifier instead.
E06.2: Put both operations in one database transaction and roll it back on failure. Check error handling so the application does not report success after rollback.
E06.3: No. It may help with syntax and types, but query plans, tenant predicates and permission rules remain engineering responsibilities.
Technical reading: [PGSQL], [KYSELY].

exercises.answer: The left join preserves one row for that customer, with NULL right-side values. Count a nonnullable right-side identifier instead.

exercises.answer: Put both operations in one database transaction and roll it back on failure. Check error handling so the application does not report success after rollback.

exercises.answer: No. It may help with syntax and types, but query plans, tenant predicates and permission rules remain engineering responsibilities.

definitions.definition: SQL is a language for defining, querying and modifying relational data.
definitions.example: SELECT name FROM customers reads customer names.
definitions.note: Understanding SQL is still important when a query builder generates it.

definitions.definition: A relational database organizes data into tables with relationships and integrity constraints.
definitions.example: Customers and calls are separate tables connected by customer identifiers.
definitions.note: A relationship is not automatically valid unless the relevant constraints or checks enforce it.

definitions.definition: A table organizes records into rows and columns.
definitions.example: A calls table contains each call's identifier, customer and duration.
definitions.note: A logical user-created table in a no-code app need not equal a physical database table.

definitions.definition: A row is one record in a table.
definitions.example: One row represents call 105 to customer 42.
definitions.note: What counts as one record must be defined before counting or deduplicating.

definitions.definition: A column is a named attribute of table rows with a declared representation.
definitions.example: duration_seconds stores each call's length.
definitions.note: Use suitable types and constraints instead of storing every value as arbitrary text.

definitions.definition: A schema describes data structure; in PostgreSQL it can also mean a namespace containing database objects.
definitions.example: A migration adds a status column to a table in a reporting schema.
definitions.note: Be clear whether you mean structural design or the named namespace.

definitions.definition: A primary key uniquely identifies each row and requires its key values to be non-NULL.
definitions.example: customer_id uniquely identifies a customer row.
definitions.note: A readable name is often unsuitable because names can repeat or change.

definitions.definition: A foreign key constrains references to matching values in a related table.
definitions.example: calls.customer_id references customers.id.
definitions.note: Choose deletion and update behavior deliberately rather than assuming orphan prevention is enough.

definitions.definition: SELECT retrieves values from a database query.
definitions.example: SELECT id, status FROM calls reads those two attributes.
definitions.note: Retrieve necessary fields rather than blindly exposing every column.

definitions.definition: INSERT adds new rows to a table.
definitions.example: Insert a new contact with a name and tenant identifier.
definitions.note: Database defaults and constraints still apply.

definitions.definition: UPDATE changes matching existing rows.
definitions.example: UPDATE calls SET status = 'done' WHERE id = 105 changes one call.
definitions.note: An omitted or incorrect filter can change far more rows than intended.

definitions.definition: SQL DELETE removes matching rows from a table.
definitions.example: Delete expired temporary import rows using an explicit expiration filter.
definitions.note: It is different from dropping the entire table structure.

definitions.definition: WHERE filters individual rows according to a condition.
definitions.example: WHERE status = 'done' selects completed calls.
definitions.note: Filtering a right-side column after a left join can remove unmatched left rows.

definitions.definition: ORDER BY defines the ordering of a query's result.
definitions.example: ORDER BY created_at, id gives a deterministic order when timestamps tie.
definitions.note: Without an explicit ordering, do not assume stable row order.

definitions.definition: GROUP BY forms groups of rows for aggregate calculations.
definitions.example: Group calls by agent to calculate each agent's completed-call count.
definitions.note: Choose the grouping level before interpreting a total.

definitions.definition: An aggregate computes a summary from multiple rows.
definitions.example: SUM(duration_seconds) adds durations; COUNT(id) counts non-NULL IDs.
definitions.note: COUNT(*) and COUNT(nullable_column) answer different questions.

definitions.definition: HAVING filters groups after aggregation.
definitions.example: HAVING COUNT(*) > 10 keeps groups with more than ten rows.
definitions.note: Use WHERE for row filters and HAVING for aggregate conditions.

definitions.definition: A JOIN combines rows according to a relationship or condition.
definitions.example: Join calls to customers so each call can show the customer's name.
definitions.note: Nonunique join keys can multiply results unexpectedly.

definitions.definition: An inner join returns row combinations that satisfy the join condition.
definitions.example: Customers with matching call records appear in a customers-to-calls inner join.
definitions.note: Customers without a match are absent.

definitions.definition: A left join retains every left-side row and uses NULL right-side values when no match exists.
definitions.example: Show all customers, including customers with zero calls.
definitions.note: Place matching-side filters carefully to avoid accidentally removing unmatched rows.

definitions.definition: NULL represents missing or unknown information in SQL.
definitions.example: A not-yet-finished call can have a NULL completion time.
definitions.note: Use IS NULL rather than = NULL; missing is not automatically zero.

definitions.definition: A constraint is a rule enforced by the database.
definitions.example: A CHECK constraint rejects negative duration values.
definitions.note: Application checks alone can miss competing writes; database rules add protection.

definitions.definition: Database normalization separates facts into related entities to reduce inconsistent duplication.
definitions.example: Store a customer's current name once and reference the customer from many calls.
definitions.note: This is different from numeric feature scaling in machine learning.

definitions.definition: Denormalization intentionally duplicates or precomputes data to simplify or accelerate reads.
definitions.example: Store a daily summary rather than recalculate every historical call for each dashboard load.
definitions.note: The duplicated representation needs an update and reconciliation strategy.

definitions.definition: A migration is a versioned change to database structure or data.
definitions.example: Migration 12 adds a nullable column; later migrations populate and constrain it.
definitions.note: A rollback of application code does not automatically reverse a destructive migration.

definitions.definition: An upsert inserts a row or updates an existing row when a specified conflict occurs.
definitions.example: An import updates the contact with external_id 123 instead of creating it again.
definitions.note: The conflict key must represent the intended identity.

definitions.definition: Kysely is a type-safe TypeScript SQL query builder.
definitions.example: Compose a typed join and inspect the resulting SQL when diagnosing performance.
definitions.note: It is not a database engine and does not remove the need for SQL judgment.

definitions.definition: An ORM maps application objects or models to relational persistence operations.
definitions.example: An ORM saves a Customer object as a customer-table row.
definitions.note: Convenience does not eliminate joins, transaction costs or N+1 query risks.

definitions.definition: A transaction groups database operations into one controlled unit of work.
definitions.example: Save a record change and its audit entry together.
definitions.note: A database transaction does not automatically include an external HTTP call.

definitions.definition: ACID groups four transaction properties: atomicity, consistency, isolation and durability.
definitions.example: A transaction updates an order and its audit record under defined database guarantees.
definitions.note: Each letter describes a different property, not simply that the database is fast or secure.

definitions.definition: Atomicity means a transaction's changes commit together or are not committed.
definitions.example: If creating an audit entry fails, the associated record update rolls back too.
definitions.note: This guarantee is limited to the transaction's participating resources.

definitions.definition: Consistency means committed transactions preserve the database's defined rules and constraints.
definitions.example: A foreign key prevents committing a call linked to a nonexistent customer.
definitions.note: The database cannot enforce an unstated business rule automatically.

definitions.definition: Isolation defines how concurrent transactions see and affect each other's changes.
definitions.example: One transaction may read a committed snapshot while another updates records.
definitions.note: Different isolation levels provide different guarantees and retry requirements.

definitions.definition: Durability means committed changes survive failures under the database's configured guarantees.
definitions.example: A successfully committed customer update should remain after a supported recovery.
definitions.note: Backups, replication and storage configuration still matter.

definitions.definition: A parameterized query keeps executable SQL structure separate from supplied data values.
definitions.example: WHERE email = $1 binds the user's email as data instead of concatenating SQL text.
definitions.note: Dynamic table or column identifiers need separate safe handling.

lessons.title: PostgreSQL, JSONB and performance without guesswork

source.text: PostgreSQL, JSONB and performance without guesswork
Before this lesson: Lesson 6

CV connection. TableOS uses PostgreSQL 16 and hybrid JSONB storage. Your CV reports search on a 500-field table improving from 60+ seconds to 1-2 seconds through query-path rewriting and PostgreSQL tuning. [CV-2]
Understand the storage choices

PostgreSQL is a relational database that supports transactions, indexes, structured SQL queries and JSON data. JSONB stores JSON in a processed binary representation with querying and indexing support. Hybrid storage can combine stable relational columns, such as tenant IDs, with flexible JSONB field values. This is useful when users define different columns in different logical tables. [PGJSON]

An index is an additional data structure that helps locate matching rows. A B-tree often supports equality, ranges and ordered access. A GIN index can support structures such as JSONB containment or full-text search. An index only helps when the query and operator can use it; adding a generic JSONB index does not accelerate every expression involving JSON. [PGINDEX]

Full-text search matches normalized terms and supports text-oriented ranking. A tsvector represents searchable terms; a tsquery represents the query. This differs from arbitrary substring matching such as ILIKE '%word%'. Selectivity describes how much a filter narrows the data.
Read a plan before changing the database

EXPLAIN shows the database's proposed execution plan. EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) actually executes the statement and reports observations. Use care: it executes writes too, and a heavy read can still load production. Inspect plans safely on representative data. [PGEXPLAIN]

A sequential scan reads through table data; an index scan uses an index to locate candidates. A sequential scan is not always wrong: reading most rows can make it reasonable. Compare estimated and actual row counts, repeated loops, sorting, buffer reads and total time. Statistics help the optimizer estimate data distribution.
Worked example: find the optimization question
Suppose a teaching table stores tenant_id, id and data JSONB. Users search status for one tenant.

SELECT id
   FROM records
   WHERE tenant_id = $1
     AND data->>'status' = $2
   ORDER BY id
   LIMIT 50;

->> extracts text. A possible candidate index is (tenant_id, (data->>'status'), id). That is a hypothesis to benchmark, not a claim about your original TableOS fix. Its usefulness depends on distribution, query frequency and write cost. A query using a different expression or scanning all tenants may need a different plan.

A connection pool reuses a bounded number of database connections. Count connections across all API and worker replicas, not just one process. Lock contention occurs when operations wait on incompatible locks. A deadlock is a cycle of operations waiting on each other; the database may abort one transaction. Keep transactions short and handle retryable failures deliberately.
Explain your actual achievement carefully

A defensible CV-based answer is: "The search path over a wide dynamic table was taking over 60 seconds. I rewrote the query path and tuned PostgreSQL, bringing it to about 1-2 seconds. Before describing the exact index or configuration, I would verify the implementation and the benchmark conditions."

Do not invent the original execution plan. Prepare what you know: query shape, row/field counts, dataset, hardware, cache state, repeated runs and correctness checks. P50 is the median; P95 is a latency value below which about 95% of observations fall. One successful run is not a P95 measurement.

Why not add RAM immediately? More hardware can help, but cannot reliably repair unnecessary repeated work, missing filters or lock problems. Why not index everything? Indexes consume storage and add write maintenance.
Memory cue: Measure -> inspect plan -> change one cause -> remeasure -> verify correct results.
Practice before reading the answers

E07.2: Four replicas each have 25 database connections. What is their combined maximum, before workers and administration?

E07.2: 100 connections. Reserve capacity for other components and avoid sizing each replica in isolation.

reading.heading: Understand the storage choices
