definitions.definition: Business intelligence turns business data into reports and analyses used for decisions.
definitions.example: Compare weekly call outcomes across teams.
definitions.note: A polished dashboard can still be wrong if the underlying metric is poorly defined.

definitions.definition: Power BI is Microsoft's platform for data modeling, reporting and interactive analytical visualizations.
definitions.example: Build a management report that filters operational results by period and team.
definitions.note: A visualization's value depends on the model, data freshness and access rules.

definitions.definition: A semantic data model organizes business entities, relationships and calculation meanings for analysis.
definitions.example: Define that call.agent_id relates to agents.id and how conversion is calculated.
definitions.note: The same label should not silently refer to different denominators in different reports.

definitions.definition: Power Query provides data-connection and transformation capabilities used in tools such as Power BI.
definitions.example: Clean imported columns and combine monthly files before reporting.
definitions.note: Data preparation is distinct from calculations evaluated within a report's filter context.

definitions.definition: DAX is an expression language for calculations in tabular data models such as those used by Power BI.
definitions.example: Define a measure that divides qualified calls by attempted calls.
definitions.note: A measure's result depends on the current model and filter context.

definitions.definition: A measure calculates a value from data in the current analytical context.
definitions.example: A Total Calls measure changes when the report is filtered to one month.
definitions.note: It is not necessarily a permanently stored value for every source row.

definitions.definition: A calculated column produces a value for each row in a data model.
definitions.example: Assign a call-duration category to each stored call row.
definitions.note: Do not confuse row-by-row calculated values with a context-dependent aggregate measure.

definitions.definition: Filter context is the set of data restrictions under which an analytical calculation is evaluated.
definitions.example: A report selection limits a conversion-rate measure to one campaign in October.
definitions.note: Changing filters can change both numerator and denominator.

definitions.definition: A dashboard presents a selected set of indicators or views for monitoring and exploration.
definitions.example: Leadership sees call totals, response time and reporting status together.
definitions.note: The word dashboard does not imply the underlying data is real-time.

definitions.definition: A report presents information organized around a question, audience or reporting period.
definitions.example: A monthly operations report includes totals, comparisons and explanations.
definitions.note: State date boundaries, exclusions and freshness.

definitions.definition: A KPI is a defined measure used to track progress toward a business objective.
definitions.example: Measure the share of qualified calls out of attempted calls.
definitions.note: A useful KPI specifies its formula, population, period and target.

definitions.definition: Streamlit is a Python framework for building interactive data applications.
definitions.example: Create a small app that filters an uploaded dataset and shows a chart.
definitions.note: Its execution and state model differs from a conventional persistent frontend component tree.

definitions.definition: A widget is an interactive control such as a selector, slider or input box.
definitions.example: A date-range widget changes which records an analyst views.
definitions.note: Validate widget input before using it in sensitive backend operations.

definitions.definition: Session state preserves selected values for one user's interaction session.
definitions.example: Keep a selected dataset or a multistep form's values while the user interacts.
definitions.note: Session state is not a shared durable business database.

definitions.definition: A cohort is a group of entities sharing a defined starting event or characteristic.
definitions.example: Users who first signed up in January form a signup cohort.
definitions.note: Choose the starting event before comparing groups.

definitions.definition: Retention measures how much of a defined starting group remains active or returns under a specified rule.
definitions.example: If 40 of 100 January signups return in February, that month's cohort retention is 40%.
definitions.note: Different activity definitions produce different retention numbers.

definitions.definition: Churn measures departures or loss from a defined population over a specified period.
definitions.example: Count subscribed customers who cancel during a month.
definitions.note: It equals one minus retention only when the populations and definitions are compatible.

definitions.definition: A cohort matrix compares groups over elapsed periods since their start.
definitions.example: Rows are signup months; columns are month 0, month 1 and month 2 retention.
definitions.note: Compare equal ages, not only equal calendar dates.

definitions.definition: Right censoring means later outcomes are not yet observed for some members of a dataset.
definitions.example: A cohort created last week has no observed three-month retention yet.
definitions.note: An unobserved future period should not be recorded as zero retention.

definitions.definition: A compliance audit examines evidence against specified policies, obligations or control requirements.
definitions.example: Reconcile reported beneficiary totals with permitted source records and required evidence.
definitions.note: The CV mentions audit work but does not provide the exact control checklist.

definitions.definition: Reconciliation compares records or totals from different stages and explains discrepancies.
definitions.example: Check that imported, rejected and pending records account for the source total.
definitions.note: A matching grand total can still hide offsetting record-level errors.

definitions.definition: Data completeness measures whether required records or fields are present.
definitions.example: Determine whether all expected daily files arrived before producing a weekly report.
definitions.note: Complete data can still contain inaccurate values.

definitions.definition: Data accuracy measures how closely stored values represent the intended real-world facts.
definitions.example: Confirm that a beneficiary's recorded date matches the verified source.
definitions.note: Accuracy and completeness are separate quality properties.

lessons.title: React, components, state and Vite

source.text: React, components, state and Vite
Before this lesson: Lessons 1, 4-5
CV connection. Your CV lists React, React 19 in project stacks, JavaScript, TypeScript and Vite for TableOS and One System. [CV-1, CV-2]
Build the screen from understandable pieces

HTML describes page structure; CSS describes appearance; JavaScript supplies behavior. The DOM, document object model, is the browser's representation of the page. These are supporting foundations for the frontend tools in your CV.

React is a library for building interfaces from components. A component is a reusable unit describing part of the UI. JSX is syntax for expressing UI-like structures inside JavaScript/TypeScript. Props are inputs passed to a component. State is component- owned information that changes over time. A render computes what the UI should look like from current inputs/state. [REACT]

A hook lets a function component use React features. useState stores state; useEffect synchronizes with external systems; useRef keeps a mutable reference without causing a render on every change. useMemo and useCallback can help reuse selected values/ functions, but should not substitute for sound state design.
Worked component: predict the screen
This snippet belongs inside a React/TypeScript project.
import { useState } from "react";

Initially the label shows 0. Each click requests an update from the previous value. React then renders the next UI. State is not changed by directly editing the visible text. The functional update is useful when the next value depends on the previous one.

Derived state is a value computed from other state. If firstName and lastName already exist, a full name can often be calculated during render rather than separately stored and synchronized. Lifting state up puts shared state in the nearest common owner so children stay consistent. [REACT]
Use effects for external synchronization

An effect may subscribe to a WebSocket, attach a browser listener or coordinate a non- React system. Cleanup removes subscriptions or cancels appropriate work when needed. Do not use an effect merely to compute a value that follows directly from props.

A key identifies an item in a rendered list across updates. Stable record IDs are usually preferable to array positions when rows can move. Virtualization renders only visible rows plus a buffer, useful for large tables. It reduces browser rendering work; it does not reduce a backend query unless the data-loading design also changes.

Vite provides development/build tooling, including a dev server and production asset build. Hot module replacement updates changed modules during development. A bundle is the processed set of frontend assets delivered to users. Vite is not a database or production API server. [VITE]
Why React and why not put all state globally?

React supports composable interfaces and a broad ecosystem. A global store is useful for genuinely shared client state, but storing every input globally creates coupling. Keep local state local and distinguish it from server-owned data, which Lesson 28 explains.

Interview bridge: "I think about state ownership and the complete data path. Optimizing a grid means coordinating backend filtering, data fetching, stable keys and rendering, rather than adding memoization everywhere."
Memory cue: Props arrive; state belongs; render derives; effects synchronize.
Practice before reading the answers
E27.1: After three clicks, what does the example show?
E27.2: Should a derived full name usually require a separate effect and state variable?
E27.3: Does virtualizing 100,000 rows automatically make the database query cheap?
Check your answers
E27.1: Calls reviewed: 3, assuming the component remained mounted and no other state changes occurred.
E27.2: Usually no. Calculate it from the existing names unless there is a specific reason to store a distinct value.
E27.3: No. It reduces rendered DOM work. Server-side filtering, pagination, serialization and data transfer still require attention.
Technical reading: [REACT], [VITE].

definitions.example: Use a heading, form label and button to structure a reporting screen.
definitions.note: Meaningful elements improve accessibility as well as visual organization.

definitions.definition: CSS controls the presentation of HTML content, such as spacing, typography and layout.
definitions.example: Use a grid layout to arrange dashboard cards.
definitions.note: Styling a control does not implement its backend permission rules.

definitions.definition: The DOM is the browser's programmatic tree representation of a document.
definitions.example: A button element has text, attributes and a place in the document tree.
definitions.note: Updating the DOM is different from updating a server-side database.

definitions.definition: React is a JavaScript library for describing user interfaces through components and state.
definitions.example: Render a reporting dashboard from the current records and filters.
definitions.note: React does not replace authentication, database storage or backend validation.

definitions.definition: A component is a reusable part of an interface with defined inputs and behavior.
definitions.example: A ReportCard displays one metric and its label.
definitions.note: Choose boundaries around coherent responsibilities, not just arbitrary file sizes.

definitions.definition: JSX is a syntax extension that allows markup-like UI expressions in JavaScript.
definitions.example: A React component returns <button>Save</button>.
definitions.note: JSX is transformed by tooling; it is not a plain HTML string.

definitions.definition: Props are inputs passed to a React component by its parent.
definitions.example: A parent passes total={12} to a ReportCard.
definitions.note: Treat props as read-only; ask the owner to change the underlying value.

definitions.definition: State is information a component retains that can influence what it renders.
definitions.example: A search input stores the current query text.
definitions.note: Changing a normal local variable alone does not schedule a React update.

definitions.definition: Rendering evaluates components to determine the interface for the current inputs and state.
definitions.example: Changing a selected filter causes React to calculate the next UI.
definitions.note: Rendering does not mean every DOM element must be replaced.

definitions.definition: In React, reconciliation determines how a newly described UI relates to the previous one.
definitions.example: React identifies which list items remain and which have changed.
definitions.note: Stable item identity helps React preserve the correct component state.

definitions.definition: A Hook is a function that lets a React component use features such as state, references or effects.
definitions.example: useState stores a value used by the component.
definitions.note: Follow Hook calling rules so React can associate state consistently across renders.

definitions.definition: useState provides a state value and a function for scheduling its update.
definitions.example: Use setCount(c => c + 1) when the next count depends on the previous count.
definitions.note: State is a snapshot for a render; calling the setter does not rewrite that snapshot immediately.

definitions.definition: useEffect synchronizes a component with an external system after a committed render, according to dependencies.
definitions.example: Subscribe to a WebSocket and clean up the subscription when dependencies change.
definitions.note: Do not use an effect merely to derive a value that can be calculated while rendering.

definitions.definition: Effect cleanup undoes a subscription or resource setup associated with an effect.
definitions.example: Remove an event listener when its component unmounts or the subscription changes.
definitions.note: Missing cleanup can duplicate listeners or leak resources.

definitions.definition: useRef stores a mutable reference that persists across renders without triggering a render when changed.
definitions.example: Keep a reference to an input element for focusing it.
definitions.note: A ref is not a replacement for state that must update the screen.

definitions.definition: useMemo caches a calculated value between renders when its dependencies remain suitable for reuse.
definitions.example: Reuse an expensive filtered view calculation when its inputs have not changed.
definitions.note: It is an optimization, not a substitute for correct state and dependency design.

definitions.definition: useCallback preserves a function identity between renders while its dependencies remain unchanged.
definitions.example: Pass a stable callback to a component whose memoization depends on reference equality.
definitions.note: Wrapping every function is not automatically beneficial.

definitions.definition: Derived state is a value that can be calculated from existing props or state.
definitions.example: The number of selected rows is selectedIds.length.
definitions.note: Storing a second independently updated copy can create inconsistencies.

definitions.definition: Lifting state moves shared state to the nearest appropriate common owner.
definitions.example: A parent holds a selected filter used by a table and a summary card.
definitions.note: Not every state value must be moved to a global store.

definitions.definition: A React list key identifies an item among its siblings across renders.
definitions.example: Use a stable record ID when rendering a changing list of customers.
definitions.note: Array position can identify the wrong item when rows are inserted or reordered.

definitions.definition: Virtualization renders only a visible subset of a large list or grid plus a small buffer.
definitions.example: Display 30 visible rows from a dataset of thousands.
definitions.note: It reduces rendered UI work, not the need for backend pagination or authorization.

definitions.definition: Vite is frontend development and build tooling used to serve and bundle web applications.
definitions.example: Run a React app during development and create production build assets.
definitions.note: Vite is neither the React library nor your production business API.

definitions.definition: HMR updates changed modules during development without requiring a complete page reload in supported cases.
definitions.example: Editing a component updates the development page quickly.
definitions.note: Development convenience does not describe how production releases are deployed.

definitions.definition: A bundle is a build artifact that packages application modules and related assets for delivery.
definitions.example: The production build produces JavaScript and CSS files for a browser to load.
definitions.note: Larger bundles can increase load time; split and cache intentionally.

lessons.title: TanStack Query/Router, Zustand, Tailwind CSS and Recharts

source.text: TanStack Query/Router, Zustand, Tailwind CSS and Recharts
Before this lesson: Lessons 4-5, 27
CV connection. Every tool in this lesson is explicitly listed in your frontend skills or project stacks. [CV-1, CV-2]
Separate three kinds of application state

Server state is data owned by the backend, such as records or reports. It can change without the current browser knowing. Client state is UI-owned information, such as an open sidebar or selected unsaved filter. URL state is navigation information encoded in the address, such as a table ID or shareable search filter.

TanStack Query manages asynchronous server-state fetching, caching and synchronization. A query key identifies cached data. A mutation changes server data. Invalidation marks affected cache entries for refresh under the application's policy. Stale data may still be displayed while a refresh occurs; stale does not necessarily mean useless. [QUERY]

TanStack Router manages route matching and typed navigation/search parameters. A route parameter identifies a part of the path, such as /tables/:id; a search parameter is a query-string value, such as ?status=open. A route guard can improve UX, but backend permissions remain mandatory. [ROUTER]

Zustand is a client-state management library using stores and subscriptions. A selector reads the state slice a component needs. Avoid copying all server data into a second store without a synchronization plan. [ZUSTAND]
Worked state placement for TableOS

The user opens table 42, filters to open tasks, edits a record and sees a success toast. Put the table ID and shareable filters in the URL where appropriate. Put fetched rows in the server-data cache. Put an unsaved editor draft and open-modal state locally or in a suitable client store. Persist the real edit through the API, then update/invalidate affected query data.

A cache key could conceptually include records, authorized tenant identity, table ID, filter and page cursor. Missing filters or tenant scope can cause stale/wrong results. Clear or partition private caches on account changes. Query keys do not replace server authorization.

An optimistic update updates the UI before server confirmation. It can feel fast but requires rollback/reconciliation on failure. A success toast must not appear merely because the local cache changed.
Styling and charts are different responsibilities

Tailwind CSS is a utility-first CSS framework: small classes describe spacing, layout, colors and responsive behavior. Responsive design adapts layout to available space. A design token standardizes choices such as spacing or colors; utility classes are most effective when used consistently. [TAILWIND]

Recharts is a charting library for React. It turns supplied data into chart components. It does not decide whether your SQL aggregation or business metric is correct. Label axes, units and periods; handle empty data and provide accessible explanations. [RECHARTS]
Explain the alternatives

Why TanStack Query rather than only useEffect? It can organize caching, loading/ error states and refetching that would otherwise be custom logic. For a tiny one-off request, simpler code may suffice.

Why Zustand rather than putting everything in Context? A store can make shared state and selective subscriptions convenient. React Context may be enough for small, low-frequency shared values. Why Tailwind rather than custom CSS everywhere? It can improve consistency and speed; it also requires discipline to avoid unreadable duplication. Why Recharts rather than raw SVG? Components reduce routine chart work, while custom graphics may justify lower-level control.
Memory cue: URL locates; Query fetches; Zustand holds UI state; Tailwind styles; Recharts visualizes.
Practice before reading the answers
E28.1: Where should authoritative customer revenue live: a backend/database or only a Zustand store?
E28.2: What should happen when an optimistic edit is rejected by the API?
E28.3: Can a correct-looking chart still show an incorrect KPI?
Check your answers
E28.1: The authoritative value belongs in the backend/database; the browser may cache or display it. Client state is not the source of truth for shared business records.
E28.2: Revert or reconcile the optimistic state, show the real error and allow an appropriate retry. Do not leave the UI falsely showing a saved result.
E28.3: Yes. Chart rendering and metric correctness are separate. Validate the underlying aggregation, filters, units and time boundaries.
Technical reading: [QUERY], [ROUTER], [ZUSTAND], [TAILWIND], [RECHARTS].

exercises.answer: The authoritative value belongs in the backend/database; the browser may cache or display it. Client state is not the source of truth for shared business records.

exercises.question: What should happen when an optimistic edit is rejected by the API?
exercises.answer: Revert or reconcile the optimistic state, show the real error and allow an appropriate retry. Do not leave the UI falsely showing a saved result.

exercises.question: Can a correct-looking chart still show an incorrect KPI?
exercises.answer: Yes. Chart rendering and metric correctness are separate. Validate the underlying aggregation, filters, units and time boundaries.

definitions.definition: Client state is information owned by the user interface rather than the authoritative server.
definitions.example: Track whether a sidebar is open or which unsaved tab is selected.
definitions.note: Do not treat client state as proof of a user's permissions.

definitions.definition: Server state is data whose authoritative source lives outside the client, usually on a backend.
definitions.example: A customer's saved status is fetched from an API.
definitions.note: It can become stale while the client is displaying it.

definitions.definition: URL state encodes navigable application choices in a path or query string.
definitions.example: A reports URL contains a selected month and page cursor.
definitions.note: Do not place secrets or unnecessary personal information in URLs.

definitions.definition: TanStack Query manages fetching, caching and updating asynchronous server data for applications.
definitions.example: Cache the API result for the current tenant's reports and refetch after a relevant change.
definitions.note: It manages client-side server-data state; it does not replace your database.

definitions.definition: A query key identifies which cached server-data result a query represents.
definitions.example: Use a key containing reports, tenant ID, period and filters.
definitions.note: Omitting a relevant input can reuse the wrong result; permissions still belong on the server.

definitions.definition: In client data tools, a mutation performs a change to server-owned data.
definitions.example: Submit an update to a record's status.
definitions.note: A successful local optimistic display is not proof the server accepted the write.

definitions.definition: Cache invalidation marks cached data as no longer reliable enough to reuse without updating it.
definitions.example: After a record update, invalidate the affected list or refresh its cached item.
definitions.note: Invalidating everything may be correct but unnecessarily expensive.

definitions.definition: TanStack Router manages application routes, navigation and related route state.
definitions.example: Navigate to a record-detail page with validated search parameters.
definitions.note: Routing selects a screen; it does not authorize its backend data.

definitions.definition: A route maps a URL pattern to an application's screen or handler.
definitions.example: /reports/:id opens the screen for a specified report.
definitions.note: An identifier in a route is untrusted input, not permission to read that object.

definitions.definition: Zustand is a state-management library for application-owned client state.
definitions.example: A store tracks open panels and selected rows across components.
definitions.note: Avoid duplicating server-data caching logic without a reason.

definitions.definition: A store holds shared application state and operations that change it.
definitions.example: Several components read the same selected-record IDs.
definitions.note: Shared state should have clear ownership and update rules.

definitions.definition: A selector chooses the part of stored state a component or calculation needs.
definitions.example: A component subscribes only to sidebarOpen rather than the entire store.
definitions.note: Unstable selection results can cause unnecessary updates depending on the subscription setup.

definitions.definition: An optimistic UI update displays an expected successful result before the server confirms it.
definitions.example: Show a changed status immediately while the API request is pending.
definitions.note: Handle rollback or reconciliation when validation, authorization or conflicts reject the write.

definitions.definition: Tailwind CSS is a utility-first CSS framework for composing interface styles.
definitions.example: Combine spacing, layout and text utilities to style a card.
definitions.note: Utility classes do not guarantee a consistent or accessible design by themselves.

definitions.definition: Responsive design adapts an interface to different viewport sizes and input conditions.
definitions.example: A two-column learning page becomes a single column on a phone.
definitions.note: Test readable text, usable controls and overflow rather than only shrinking the layout.

definitions.definition: A design token is a named reusable value for visual decisions such as colors, spacing or typography.
definitions.example: Use one spacing token for padding across related cards.
definitions.note: Tokens support consistency; they do not replace layout judgment.

definitions.definition: Recharts is a React charting library for presenting data through chart components.
definitions.example: Render a line chart of weekly completed calls.
definitions.note: The chart must preserve the meaning of units, filters and missing observations.

definitions.definition: SVG is a vector-graphics format used for shapes and diagrams, including many web charts.
definitions.example: A chart line is described as scalable geometric paths.
definitions.note: Scalable geometry does not automatically make labels readable on a small screen.

definitions.definition: Accessibility makes an interface usable by people with different abilities and assistive technologies.
definitions.example: Provide labeled inputs, keyboard navigation and a text explanation of a chart.
definitions.note: Color alone should not be the only way to distinguish success from failure.

lessons.title: Cloud infrastructure, Docker, AWS and Google Cloud

source.text: Cloud infrastructure, Docker, AWS and Google Cloud
Before this lesson: Lessons 1, 5-11

CV connection. Your CV lists GCP, AWS EC2/S3, Docker and containerized model/API deployment. TableOS also names Google Cloud Storage. No production Kubernetes or Terraform implementation is stated. [CV-1, CV-2]
Define infrastructure from the ground up

A server provides compute, memory, storage and network access for applications. A virtual machine, VM, is a software-defined machine running a guest operating system. Cloud computing rents managed infrastructure/services instead of requiring you to own every physical machine. A region is a provider's geographic deployment area; availability/failure domains within it help structure resilience.

AWS, Amazon Web Services, and GCP, Google Cloud Platform, are cloud ecosystems. EC2 provides virtual compute instances. S3 is object storage. Google Cloud Storage, GCS, is Google's object-storage service. An object stores file-like bytes plus metadata in a bucket. Object storage is not a relational database or a drop-in local disk for every workload. [AWS, S3, GCS]

IAM, identity and access management, controls cloud identities and permissions. A service account or workload identity represents software. A secret is sensitive configuration, such as a credential. A signed URL can grant time-limited access to an object under defined conditions; treat it as a capability that must not be exposed carelessly.
Docker without confusing images and containers

A Docker image is a packaged filesystem/configuration used to start an application. A container is a running isolated process environment based on an image. A Dockerfile describes how to build an image. A registry stores/distributes images. A volume persists selected data independently of a container's writable layer. [DOCKER]

Containers commonly share the host kernel; they are not identical to VMs or automatically a safe sandbox for hostile code. Use least privilege, suitable isolation, resource limits, patched dependencies and restricted network access. Do not bake credentials into image layers.
Worked deployment layout

Teaching layout: a React asset host serves the UI; an API container handles authorized requests; PostgreSQL stores business records; Redis supports jobs/cache; workers perform imports; object storage holds uploaded documents. An AI model may be accessed remotely or deployed separately. This describes roles, not your verified exact cloud topology.

When a container is replaced, its local writable data may disappear. Keep durable documents in suitable storage and durable records in the database. A health check reports whether the process is alive; a readiness check reports whether it should receive traffic. These checks should reflect meaningful state without causing unnecessary cascading restarts.

A load balancer distributes requests across instances. A reverse proxy receives requests and forwards them to internal services. TLS encrypts transport and authenticates endpoints through certificates. These mechanisms do not replace application authorization.
Backups, monitoring and scaling choices

A backup is a recoverable copy; a restore test proves it can be used. RPO, recovery point objective, is tolerable data loss measured in time. RTO, recovery time objective, is tolerable recovery duration. Storing a backup is not equivalent to achieving either objective.

Logs record events; metrics measure quantities; traces connect operations across a request. Observability uses them to understand internal behavior. Monitor queue delay, database pressure, request errors, model latency and cost, with appropriate privacy controls.

Why managed services? They can reduce operational work, at cost/control trade-offs. Why not Kubernetes automatically? Container orchestration can help at suitable scale but adds complexity. Your CV supports Docker/cloud work; distinguish theoretical knowledge from actual cluster operations.
Memory cue: Compute runs; database records; object storage holds files; IAM limits; monitoring observes; backups recover.
Practice before reading the answers
E29.1: What happens to a PDF saved only inside a replaceable container?
E29.2: Should the browser receive an unrestricted cloud service-account key?
E29.3: Why does a successful backup job not prove recovery works?
Check your answers
E29.1: It may be lost with the container unless correctly persisted. Store durable files in object storage or an appropriate persistent volume and test retrieval permissions.
E29.2: No. Keep privileged credentials on trusted infrastructure and expose narrowly authorized operations or short-lived scoped capabilities.
E29.3: The backup may be incomplete, incompatible or impossible to restore quickly. Perform restore exercises and verify both data correctness and recovery time.
Technical reading: [DOCKER], [AWS], [S3], [GCS].

exercises.answer: It may be lost with the container unless correctly persisted. Store durable files in object storage or an appropriate persistent volume and test retrieval permissions.

exercises.question: Should the browser receive an unrestricted cloud service-account key?
exercises.answer: No. Keep privileged credentials on trusted infrastructure and expose narrowly authorized operations or short-lived scoped capabilities.

exercises.question: Why does a successful backup job not prove recovery works?
exercises.answer: The backup may be incomplete, incompatible or impossible to restore quickly. Perform restore exercises and verify both data correctness and recovery time.

definitions.definition: Cloud computing provides computing resources as services rather than requiring all infrastructure to be owned locally.
definitions.example: Rent a virtual server and managed storage for an API.
definitions.note: The application owner still has security, reliability and cost responsibilities.

definitions.definition: A virtual machine is a software-defined computing environment with its own guest operating system.
definitions.example: Run a Linux API server on a cloud VM.
definitions.note: A container typically shares a host kernel instead of running a full guest OS.

definitions.definition: Amazon Web Services is a cloud platform providing compute, storage and other infrastructure services.
definitions.example: Use an EC2 instance for an application and S3 for uploaded objects.
definitions.note: Knowing these services does not establish experience with every AWS product.

definitions.definition: Google Cloud Platform is a cloud-services platform providing compute, storage and managed services.
definitions.example: Deploy an application using Google Cloud infrastructure and object storage.
definitions.note: The CV does not provide the exact configuration of every deployment.

definitions.definition: Amazon EC2 provides configurable virtual compute instances.
definitions.example: Run an API process on a provisioned Linux instance.
definitions.note: You must manage appropriate OS, network and application controls for your setup.

definitions.definition: Amazon S3 is an object-storage service using buckets and object keys.
definitions.example: Store an uploaded CSV under a controlled object key.
definitions.note: It is not a relational database or a normal local filesystem.

definitions.definition: Google Cloud Storage is Google's object-storage service using buckets and objects.
definitions.example: Store authorized attachments for a platform.
definitions.note: Object access and public sharing must be configured deliberately.

definitions.definition: Object storage stores data as objects identified by keys, along with associated metadata.
definitions.example: Retrieve an uploaded document using its bucket and object key.
definitions.note: Database joins and in-place filesystem semantics are not its primary interface.

definitions.definition: A bucket is an object-storage container with associated configuration and access rules.
definitions.example: Keep application uploads in a private bucket.
definitions.note: An object being in a bucket does not make it private unless the access configuration does.

definitions.definition: A cloud region is a geographic area where a provider offers infrastructure.
definitions.example: Place an application near users and permitted data locations.
definitions.note: Latency, availability, cost and data-location requirements affect the choice.

definitions.definition: An availability zone is a provider-defined infrastructure location designed for separation from other zones in a region.
definitions.example: Spread supported workloads across zones to reduce one-location failure risk.
definitions.note: Provider terminology and guarantees vary; a region alone does not imply a resilient deployment.

definitions.definition: IAM controls which identities can perform which operations on cloud resources.
definitions.example: Allow an API service to read only its required storage bucket.
definitions.note: Prefer scoped service identities instead of sharing a human administrator's credentials.

definitions.definition: A service account is an identity used by a workload rather than a human user.
definitions.example: An ingestion worker accesses storage through its assigned identity.
definitions.note: Rotate or avoid long-lived keys where supported, and grant only required permissions.

definitions.definition: A secret is sensitive configuration that grants access or protects privileged operations.
definitions.example: An external API key belongs in protected server-side configuration.
definitions.note: Do not embed secrets in frontend bundles, source repositories or log messages.

definitions.definition: A signed URL grants a specified temporary operation on a resource to whoever possesses the URL.
definitions.example: Allow an authorized client to download one private file for a limited time.
definitions.note: Treat it as sensitive bearer access and restrict duration and operation.

definitions.definition: Docker is tooling for building and running applications in containers.
definitions.example: Package an API with its runtime dependencies for repeatable deployment.
definitions.note: Containerization helps consistency but is not a complete security boundary or deployment strategy.

definitions.definition: A container image is a packaged template containing filesystem layers and configuration used to start containers.
definitions.example: Build an image with the application's dependencies and startup command.
definitions.note: An image is not a running process.

definitions.definition: A container is a running or stopped instance of an image with isolated process and resource boundaries.
definitions.example: Start two API containers from the same image.
definitions.note: Containers normally share a host kernel and need deliberate resource and privilege limits.

definitions.definition: A Dockerfile describes instructions for building a container image.
definitions.example: Choose a base image, install dependencies, copy application code and set a command.
definitions.note: Avoid copying secrets and unnecessary build files into the image.

definitions.definition: A container registry stores and distributes container images.
definitions.example: A deployment retrieves a versioned image produced by CI.
definitions.note: Use authenticated access and trusted images; a tag alone may be mutable.

definitions.definition: A volume provides storage whose lifetime can be managed separately from a container's writable layer.
definitions.example: Keep database files outside an ephemeral application container.
definitions.note: A persistent volume is not automatically a tested backup.

definitions.definition: A health check tests a defined aspect of whether a service is functioning.
definitions.example: A monitoring endpoint confirms that the application can handle a basic request.
definitions.note: A process being alive does not prove that all required dependencies work.

definitions.definition: Readiness indicates whether an instance should currently receive application traffic.
definitions.example: Do not route requests to a newly started instance until initialization is complete.
definitions.note: Avoid readiness logic that causes every healthy instance to disappear unnecessarily during a shared dependency issue.

definitions.definition: A load balancer distributes traffic across eligible service instances.
definitions.example: Route API requests to several ready replicas.
definitions.note: Sessions, WebSockets and connection draining need workload-appropriate handling.

definitions.definition: A reverse proxy accepts client requests and forwards them to backend services.
definitions.example: Route /api to an internal API process while serving static frontend files.
definitions.note: Configure trusted forwarding headers and limits; do not blindly trust client-supplied proxy headers.

definitions.definition: Transport Layer Security protects a connection's confidentiality and integrity and authenticates endpoints under its certificate model.
definitions.example: HTTPS protects browser-to-server traffic in transit.
definitions.note: TLS does not fix application authorization or protect data after a compromised endpoint decrypts it.

definitions.definition: A backup is a recoverable copy of data maintained for restoration after loss or damage.
definitions.example: Restore a database snapshot into a test environment to verify it works.
definitions.note: A backup that has never been restored is an untested recovery assumption.

definitions.definition: RPO is the target maximum amount of data loss expressed as time.
definitions.example: An RPO of one hour means planning to lose no more than roughly one hour of data under the specified recovery scenario.
definitions.note: It is an objective requiring suitable backups or replication, not a guarantee by itself.

definitions.definition: RTO is the target time to restore a service after an interruption.
definitions.example: Plan to restore the reporting application within two hours.
definitions.note: Include diagnosis, restoration and validation, not only copying a backup.

definitions.definition: A log is a recorded event or message about system behavior.
definitions.example: Record a request ID and a safe summary of a failed import.
definitions.note: Avoid recording secrets or unnecessary sensitive payloads.

definitions.definition: A metric is a numerical measurement collected over time or a population.
definitions.example: Track queue depth, API error rate and p95 latency.
definitions.note: Choose definitions and labels that make the measure interpretable and affordable to collect.

definitions.definition: A trace connects spans representing work performed during a request or operation.
definitions.example: Follow one request from API to database to model provider.
definitions.note: Propagate correlation information across boundaries without exposing sensitive context.

definitions.definition: Observability is the ability to understand system behavior from collected outputs such as logs, metrics and traces.
definitions.example: Investigate whether slow answers come from retrieval, the database or model generation.
definitions.note: Collecting telemetry is useful only when it supports meaningful diagnosis.

definitions.definition: A managed service delegates specified operational responsibilities to a provider.
definitions.example: Use a managed database instead of patching its host yourself.
definitions.note: The provider's responsibilities do not remove your schema, access-control or backup-validation responsibilities.

lessons.title: Git, monorepos, CI/CD, Playwright and release quality

source.text: Git, monorepos, CI/CD, Playwright and release quality
Before this lesson: Lessons 2, 4-5, 11, 27-29

CV connection. Your CV lists GitHub Actions CI/CD, pnpm/Turborepo monorepos, Playwright, CodeQL and Semgrep. TableOS includes 20+ shared packages, 30+ server modules and 58 versioned releases. [CV-1, CV-2]
Source control and shared code

Git records versioned changes. A repository stores project history. A commit records a snapshot/change set; a branch names a line of development. A pull request proposes a change for review. A merge conflict occurs when changes cannot be combined automatically. A tag can mark a release version.

A monorepo contains multiple packages/projects in one repository. A shared package provides reusable code, such as validation or API contracts. pnpm manages JavaScript dependencies and workspaces. A workspace links related packages. Turborepo coordinates tasks across packages and can cache reusable build results. A lockfile records dependency resolution for more reproducible installs. [PNPM, TURBO]

One repository does not mean one deployment. Conversely, separate repositories do not guarantee clean architectural boundaries. Avoid a shared package that imports everything and creates circular dependencies.
CI/CD in a concrete pipeline

Continuous integration, CI, routinely integrates changes and runs automated checks. Continuous delivery keeps validated software ready for release. Continuous deployment releases validated changes automatically. GitHub Actions executes workflows triggered by events; a workflow contains jobs, jobs contain steps, and a runner executes them. [GHA]

A teaching pipeline is: install from lockfile -> type checks -> unit tests -> integration tests -> security/dependency scans -> build image/assets -> deploy staging -> smoke tests -> approved production release -> monitor.

A unit test checks a small isolated behavior. An integration test checks components working together, such as API plus database. An end-to-end test exercises a user journey. A smoke test quickly checks critical basic behavior after deployment. A fixture provides repeatable test data/setup. A mock replaces a dependency for a controlled test.
Playwright and security checks

Playwright automates browser interactions and assertions for tests. Example journey: log in -> open permitted table -> edit a field -> confirm persistence -> verify a forbidden action fails. Test both successful and denied operations. Browser tests should use deterministic data and resilient locators instead of arbitrary sleeps. [PLAYWRIGHT]

CodeQL, Semgrep and dependency auditing identify potential issues, but require triage. Keep tests for specific fixed vulnerabilities. A regression is a previously working behavior becoming broken. A flaky test inconsistently passes/fails without a relevant product change; investigate it rather than hiding every failure with retries.
Release safely when schemas change

A backward-compatible migration lets old and new application versions coexist during rollout. An expand-contract approach first adds compatible structures, migrates use/ data, then removes obsolete structures after old consumers are gone. Rolling back code does not automatically undo a destructive database migration.

A feature flag controls exposure without necessarily redeploying code. A versioned release identifies what shipped; 58 releases in your CV show iteration, not proof of a particular deployment cadence or zero incidents.

Why a monorepo? It can make shared contracts and coordinated changes easier. Why not share everything? Excessive coupling slows builds and makes ownership unclear. Why not rely on end-to-end tests alone? They are usually slower and less precise at locating small failures; use several test levels.
Memory cue: Commit -> verify -> build -> release -> observe -> recover.
Practice before reading the answers
E30.1: Which test checks that a denied user cannot export another tenant's records?
E30.2: Can reverting application code restore a dropped database column's data?
E30.3: Why preserve a lockfile in a reproducible build workflow?
Check your answers
E30.1: An integration test should verify server enforcement; an end-to-end test can also verify the UI journey. Do not rely only on whether the button is hidden.
E30.2: No. Recovery may require backups or a planned data migration. Avoid destructive changes until compatibility and recovery are understood.

E30.3: It records resolved dependency versions so different environments are less likely to build against different dependency trees. It does not eliminate every operating-system or external-service difference.
Technical reading: [GHA], [PNPM], [TURBO], [PLAYWRIGHT], [CODEQL], [SEMGREP].

exercises.answer: An integration test should verify server enforcement; an end-to-end test can also verify the UI journey. Do not rely only on whether the button is hidden.

exercises.answer: No. Recovery may require backups or a planned data migration. Avoid destructive changes until compatibility and recovery are understood.

exercises.answer: It records resolved dependency versions so different environments are less likely to build against different dependency trees. It does not eliminate every operating-system or external-service difference.

definitions.definition: Git is a distributed version-control system for recording and collaborating on file changes.
definitions.example: Commit a reviewed change to the API's source code.
definitions.note: Git tracks history; it is not the same service as GitHub.

definitions.definition: A repository contains project files and their version-control history.
definitions.example: Keep an application's code and documentation in one Git repository.
definitions.note: Secrets should not be committed even to a private repository.

definitions.definition: A commit records a versioned snapshot with metadata and relationships to earlier commits.
definitions.example: Commit a bug fix with a message explaining its purpose.
definitions.note: A commit being present does not mean it has passed tests or reached production.

definitions.definition: A branch is a movable name referring to a line of development in Git.
definitions.example: Develop a reporting fix on a separate branch before merging.
definitions.note: Branches do not isolate production databases or external side effects.

definitions.definition: A pull request proposes a code change for review and integration on a collaboration platform.
definitions.example: Review tests, security impact and migration behavior before merging.
definitions.note: Approval should evaluate correctness and risks, not just formatting.

definitions.definition: A merge conflict is a situation where Git cannot automatically combine competing changes.
definitions.example: Two branches edit the same lines differently.
definitions.note: Resolve the intended combined behavior and rerun tests, not merely remove conflict markers.

definitions.definition: A tag names a particular version-control reference, commonly used to identify a release.
definitions.example: Mark an approved revision as a specific release version.
definitions.note: A source tag alone does not prove which artifact was deployed.

definitions.definition: A monorepo stores multiple related applications or packages in one repository.
definitions.example: Keep frontend, API and shared TypeScript types together.
definitions.note: A monorepo is a code organization choice, not proof that everything deploys as one process.

definitions.definition: A shared package contains reusable code consumed by multiple parts of a system.
definitions.example: Use a common validation schema in the API and supporting tools.
definitions.note: Shared code needs ownership and compatibility discipline to avoid unintended coupling.

definitions.definition: pnpm is a package manager for JavaScript and TypeScript projects with workspace support.
definitions.example: Install project dependencies and run scripts across workspace packages.
definitions.note: The package manager is not the application runtime.

definitions.definition: A package-manager workspace groups related packages so dependencies and scripts can be managed together.
definitions.example: The API depends on a local shared-types package in the same repository.
definitions.note: Keep package boundaries explicit even when local linking is convenient.

definitions.definition: Turborepo is tooling for coordinating tasks and caching suitable work across JavaScript/TypeScript monorepos.
definitions.example: Run builds in dependency order and reuse an unchanged task's cached result.
definitions.note: Correct cache keys must account for relevant inputs and configuration.

definitions.definition: A lockfile records dependency resolution information to make installations more repeatable.
definitions.example: CI installs versions consistent with the committed dependency lockfile.
definitions.note: Reproducibility also depends on runtime, platform and build configuration.

definitions.definition: CI frequently integrates changes and automatically checks that they build and satisfy selected tests.
definitions.example: A pull request runs tests, type checks and security scans.
definitions.note: A passing pipeline only covers the checks it actually performs.

definitions.definition: Continuous delivery keeps validated software ready to release through a controlled process.
definitions.example: A successful build is packaged and waits for approval to deploy.
definitions.note: Delivery does not necessarily mean every change goes straight to production.

definitions.definition: Continuous deployment automatically releases qualifying validated changes to production.
definitions.example: A change passing defined gates is deployed without a separate manual approval step.
definitions.note: It requires reliable checks, monitoring and a recovery strategy.

definitions.definition: GitHub Actions is a platform for automating repository workflows such as tests and builds.
definitions.example: Run tests, dependency checks and an image build when a pull request changes code.
definitions.note: Review permissions and untrusted inputs before allowing a workflow to access secrets.

definitions.definition: In GitHub Actions, a workflow defines event-triggered automation composed of jobs and steps.
definitions.example: A CI workflow starts on a pull request and runs verification jobs.
definitions.note: This use of workflow is related to but distinct from a business automation workflow.

definitions.definition: In CI, a job groups steps executed on an assigned runner environment.
definitions.example: A test job installs dependencies and runs a test suite.
definitions.note: Separate jobs need explicit artifact or output transfer when they exchange data.

definitions.definition: A CI step is one command or action inside a job.
definitions.example: One step runs a type checker; the next runs unit tests.
definitions.note: A later step should not silently hide a meaningful earlier failure.

definitions.definition: A runner is the execution environment that runs CI jobs.
definitions.example: A Linux runner checks out the repository and executes build steps.
definitions.note: Self-hosted runners require isolation and maintenance, especially for untrusted changes.

definitions.definition: A unit test checks a small, focused behavior with controlled dependencies.
definitions.example: Test that a formula parser rejects a circular reference.
definitions.note: The chosen unit is a design boundary, not necessarily exactly one function.

definitions.definition: An integration test checks whether components work together across a real or realistic boundary.
definitions.example: Verify that an API creates a record and its outbox event in a database transaction.
definitions.note: Mocking every dependency would miss the integration behavior being tested.

definitions.definition: An end-to-end test exercises a user journey across the relevant application layers.
definitions.example: Log in, create a record and confirm it appears in the UI.
definitions.note: Keep tests focused and stable; a few UI journeys do not cover every backend rule.

definitions.definition: A fixture provides repeatable test data or setup and cleanup.
definitions.example: Create a tenant with one viewer and one editor before an authorization test.
definitions.note: Use synthetic data and reset state so tests do not influence one another unexpectedly.

definitions.definition: A mock replaces a real dependency with controlled behavior for a test.
definitions.example: Simulate a provider returning a timeout without making a paid API call.
definitions.note: A successful mock test does not prove the real provider integration works.

definitions.definition: Playwright is browser-automation tooling commonly used for end-to-end testing.
definitions.example: Open a page, click Submit and assert that an accessible success message appears.
definitions.note: Prefer meaningful locators and condition-based waits over arbitrary sleeps.

definitions.definition: A flaky test gives inconsistent results without a relevant intended code change.
definitions.example: A UI test sometimes checks a result before the network response arrives.
definitions.note: Investigate timing, shared state and dependencies instead of merely increasing retries.

definitions.definition: An expand-contract migration introduces a compatible schema change before removing the old representation later.
definitions.example: Add a new column, migrate readers and data, then remove the old column after compatibility is verified.
definitions.note: A rolling application deployment can otherwise mix incompatible code and schemas.

definitions.definition: A feature flag controls whether a behavior is enabled independently of the deployed code version.
definitions.example: Enable a new AI feature for a small internal test group first.
definitions.note: Flags need access control, testing and eventual cleanup.

definitions.definition: A release is an identified package of changes made available to its intended environment or users.
definitions.example: Deploy a tested image and record its source version and migration state.
definitions.note: The CV's release count does not establish a particular deployment frequency or reliability score.

lessons.title: TableOS: connect every feature to its engineering purpose

source.text: TableOS: connect every feature to its engineering purpose
Before this lesson: Lessons 4-11, 16-20, 23-24, 27-30
CV connection. This lesson preserves the TableOS claims on CV page 2. Architectural explanations are teaching material; unlisted implementation details remain unverified. [CV-2]
Start with the business problem

Your CV describes TableOS as an Airtable-class, multi-tenant collaborative no-code database platform that replaced Airtable company-wide. It reports about 96K TypeScript lines, a pnpm/Turborepo monorepo, 20+ shared packages, 30+ server modules, 34 architecture documents and 58 versioned releases. These are self-reported project facts, not external audit results.

The listed stack is TypeScript, Node.js, Fastify, PostgreSQL 16, Redis, BullMQ, WebSockets, React 19, Vite, TanStack, Zustand, Google Cloud Storage and Docker. Do not recite this as a disconnected list: explain which user requirement each component serves.
Understand the domain terms

A no-code database platform lets users define tables/fields and workflows without writing ordinary application code. A field engine defines how each field type is validated, stored, displayed, filtered and computed. Your CV says 18 field types but does not enumerate them; do not invent a list of 18. Text, number and date are teaching examples only.

A linked record represents a relationship between records. A formula engine computes values from expressions and references. A parser converts formula text into structured syntax. An AST, abstract syntax tree, represents that structure. A dependency graph tracks which values depend on others. Cycle detection finds circular dependencies; topological order evaluates a dependency before its dependents.

Worked example: subtotal = quantity * unit_price; total = subtotal + tax. A quantity change requires subtotal before total. If total also defines quantity, a cycle appears. Reject or explicitly handle it; do not endlessly recalculate. Do not implement user formulas as unrestricted eval.
Connect persistence and asynchronous behavior

The CV describes hybrid JSONB storage and a modular monolith split into API, realtime, worker and relay processes. API handles validated business operations; realtime handles connected subscribers; workers execute background tasks; relay propagates committed events. Transactional outbox plus BullMQ helps avoid losing a job when a record is committed.

Two-way Airtable/HubSpot sync is described up to 500K records and 900 fields per table with incremental refresh. Prepare the precise meaning of these limits: supported versus observed, per-table versus total, benchmark conditions and failure recovery. The CV does not establish 500K simultaneous users or calls.
Automation, security and AI features

The automation engine includes Gmail/Slack actions, conditions, loops, sandboxed scripts and dry-run tests. Describe trigger -> scoped execution identity -> conditions -> actions -> history. Audit history records changes and actors. Undo creates a controlled reversal; it may need to check whether a later edit has occurred, and it cannot necessarily unsend an email.

Security includes Google OAuth, TOTP MFA, role/field permissions, masked PII, scoped API tokens, usage logs and automated checks. AI features include a plain-language table/ automation builder, an in-app chatbot and AI-generated dashboards. A safe builder generates a structured proposed plan, validates it against supported types/permissions, previews it and commits through ordinary backend rules. This is a design explanation, not proof of your exact builder implementation.
Defend the two strongest trade-offs

Why PostgreSQL/JSONB? Dynamic fields benefit from flexible representation, while relationships, transactions and permissions benefit from relational structure. The trade-off is query/indexing complexity. Why a modular monolith? It can keep development and transactions manageable while distinct process types scale independently. The trade-off is discipline needed to maintain module boundaries.

Your search result is 60+ seconds reduced to 1-2 seconds on a 500-field table through rewriting the query path and tuning PostgreSQL. Explain the measured problem, your actual change and validation. Do not invent an index or attribute a precise percentile not in the evidence.
Memory cue: Dynamic data + reliable changes + collaboration + controlled automation + measurable performance.
Practice before reading the answers
E31.1: In the subtotal/total example, which formula recalculates first after quantity changes?
E31.2: Why is undoing a stored field different from undoing an already sent email?
E31.3: Give a 45-second TableOS explanation without listing more than five technology names.
Check your answers
E31.1: Subtotal first, then total. The dependency graph determines the order; a cycle requires explicit rejection or another defined policy.
E31.2: A stored value can often be compensated with a new authorized change. An external email cannot generally be recalled by reverting your database row.

E31.3: "I architected and co-built a collaborative, multi-tenant database platform replacing Airtable internally. It supports dynamic fields, formulas, real-time updates, automations and two-way integrations. PostgreSQL handles transactional data, while queues isolate background work. I also improved a wide-table search path from over 60 seconds to about 1-2 seconds."
Technical reading: [PGJSON], [KYSELY], [BULL], [OUTBOX], [REACT].

exercises.question: In the subtotal/total example, which formula recalculates first after quantity changes?
exercises.answer: Subtotal first, then total. The dependency graph determines the order; a cycle requires explicit rejection or another defined policy.

exercises.question: Why is undoing a stored field different from undoing an already sent email?
exercises.answer: A stored value can often be compensated with a new authorized change. An external email cannot generally be recalled by reverting your database row.

exercises.question: Give a 45-second TableOS explanation without listing more than five technology names.
exercises.answer: "I architected and co-built a collaborative, multi-tenant database platform replacing Airtable internally. It supports dynamic fields, formulas, real-time updates, automations and two-way integrations. PostgreSQL handles transactional data, while queues isolate background work. I also improved a wide-table search path from over 60 seconds to about 1-2 seconds."

lessons.memory: Dynamic data + reliable changes + collaboration + controlled automation + measurable performance.

definitions.definition: TableOS is the CV's Airtable-class collaborative database platform, architected and co-built using a TypeScript-centered stack.
definitions.example: Use its record-editing flow to explain frontend, API, PostgreSQL, permissions and realtime updates together.
definitions.note: Its stated features and results come from the CV; detailed examples here are teaching illustrations.

definitions.definition: A no-code platform lets users configure supported applications or data workflows without writing conventional application code.
definitions.example: A user creates a Status field and a notification rule through an interface.
definitions.note: The platform itself still requires substantial software engineering.

definitions.definition: In a table-oriented application, a base groups related tables and their configuration.
definitions.example: A customer-operations base contains Contacts, Companies and Calls tables.
definitions.note: The exact TableOS ownership hierarchy must match your implementation, not an assumed Airtable copy.

definitions.definition: A record represents one stored entity or entry within a table.
definitions.example: One contact record has a name, phone number and status.
definitions.note: A record ID should remain stable even when its displayed name changes.

definitions.definition: A field defines a named attribute and its behavior within a table.
definitions.example: A Status field accepts permitted select options.
definitions.note: Field metadata and each record's stored field value are different things.

definitions.definition: A field engine implements the behavior of supported field types, including validation, storage and display rules.
definitions.example: A date field validates dates while a numeric field supports numeric operations.
definitions.note: The CV states 18 types but does not enumerate their exact names.

definitions.definition: A linked record expresses a relationship between entries in different tables or logical collections.
definitions.example: A Call record links to its Contact record.
definitions.note: Links need integrity and permission rules; a display name alone is not a reliable relationship key.

definitions.definition: A formula is an expression that calculates a result from values and supported operations.
definitions.example: Quantity multiplied by Unit Price gives a line total.
definitions.note: User formulas must not become unrestricted execution of arbitrary application code.

definitions.definition: A formula engine parses, validates and evaluates supported expressions and their dependencies.
definitions.example: Recalculate Total when Quantity or Unit Price changes.
definitions.note: It needs explicit error, type and dependency behavior.

definitions.definition: A formula tokenizer splits expression text into meaningful units such as numbers, names and operators.
definitions.example: 'A + 2' becomes a field reference, a plus operator and a numeric literal.
definitions.note: These tokens are not necessarily the subword tokens used by an LLM.

definitions.definition: A parser converts a sequence of tokens into a structure that follows a defined grammar.
definitions.example: Recognize multiplication inside a sum before evaluating the expression.
definitions.note: Parsing checks structure; authorization and allowed-operation checks are additional steps.

definitions.definition: An AST is a tree describing an expression or program's logical structure without every surface-formatting detail.
definitions.example: A + B * 2 has an addition node whose right child is a multiplication node.
definitions.note: An AST enables controlled interpretation instead of unsafe text evaluation.

definitions.definition: A dependency graph connects items to the other items they rely on.
definitions.example: Total depends on Quantity and Unit Price; Grand Total depends on Total.
definitions.note: Knowing dependencies helps recalculate only affected results.

definitions.definition: A cycle is a path in a graph that returns to an earlier node.
definitions.example: A depends on B and B depends on A.
definitions.note: A simple formula engine normally rejects circular dependencies rather than recalculating forever.

definitions.definition: A topological ordering arranges a directed acyclic graph so each dependency is processed before its dependent.
definitions.example: Calculate line totals before calculating a grand total that uses them.
definitions.note: A graph containing a cycle does not have such an ordering for all its nodes.

definitions.definition: Hybrid JSONB storage combines relational metadata or constraints with flexible JSONB record values.
definitions.example: Store stable record identity relationally while user-defined values live in JSONB.
definitions.note: This is a storage approach, not proof of the exact schema used in your production system.

definitions.definition: The CV describes an outbox that records events alongside business changes before a relay feeds background work.
definitions.example: A teaching write transaction updates a record and inserts its change event together.
definitions.note: Relay retries still require safe handling of duplicate publication or consumption.

definitions.definition: Audit history records significant changes and their associated identity, time and context.
definitions.example: Show which authorized user changed a status from New to Contacted.
definitions.note: Audit records should be protected and should not expose unnecessary sensitive values.

definitions.definition: Undo creates a controlled reversal of an earlier action when the application permits it.
definitions.example: Restore a prior field value while recording the reversal as a new event.
definitions.note: Concurrent edits, permissions and external side effects can make a reversal nontrivial.

definitions.definition: A scoped API token grants a defined subset of application access to an integration or user.
definitions.example: Allow an integration to read one base without managing all users.
definitions.note: Enforce scopes server-side and provide revocation and safe auditing.

definitions.definition: PII masking hides or substitutes personal-data values in a permitted display or output.
definitions.example: A viewer sees a partially hidden phone number.
definitions.note: Masking in the UI is insufficient when an API still returns the unmasked value.

definitions.definition: A plain-language builder converts a user's natural-language request into a proposed application configuration.
definitions.example: A user asks for a tasks table with owner, due date and status fields.
definitions.note: Validate the proposed structure and permissions before applying it.

definitions.definition: An AI-generated dashboard uses a model to propose or assemble analytical views from authorized data and supported components.
definitions.example: Propose a weekly call-outcome chart using a defined reporting query.
definitions.note: The model should not invent numbers, permissions or unsupported visual components.

definitions.definition: A search optimization claim describes a measured improvement under a stated workload.
definitions.example: Your CV reports search improving from over 60 seconds to about 1-2 seconds on a 500-field table.
definitions.note: The supplied source does not identify the exact query rewrite, indexes or benchmark conditions.

definitions.definition: A capacity claim describes an amount of data or workload a system is intended or observed to handle.
definitions.example: The CV mentions synchronization of up to 500K records and 900 fields per table.
definitions.note: Total records are not concurrent users, requests per second or independently verified load-test results.

lessons.title: One System: reports, live-data tools and permission-aware AI

source.text: One System: reports, live-data tools and permission-aware AI
Before this lesson: Lessons 5-11, 16, 19-20, 23-28
CV connection. All project facts in this lesson come from One System on CV page 2. Proposed traces and safety checks are educational elaboration. [CV-2]
What the platform does

Your CV describes One System as the company's central data, reporting and AI platform. Its stack includes Python, Flask, PostgreSQL, JWT, Socket.IO, OpenAI GPT-4o, HubSpot, Google Ads, Slack, React 19, Vite, Tailwind CSS and Recharts. It reports 120+ REST endpoints, pooled database connections and dashboards used by project managers and leadership.

Reporting spans marketing, Google Ads, AI calls, design and QA. The platform includes AI summarizers, integrations, notifications and PDF/CSV export, with approximately 70% less manual reporting. This metric should be tied to an actual baseline and measurement method before a detailed interview discussion.
Define the reporting architecture

A source system owns original records, such as ad metrics or call outcomes. A reporting layer combines authorized data into defined metrics. A semantic definition explains what a measure means, including filters, time periods and exclusions. A summary expresses those results for a reader; it should not independently invent numbers.

Tool calling over live reports differs from embedding every fact into a vector database. Structured totals change frequently and can be queried deterministically. A retrieval system may help explain policies or definitions, while a report tool calculates authoritative current values.
Worked question: "How did our calls perform this week?"

A safe teaching path is: resolve the user's team and allowed reports; determine the business timezone and period; call an authorized backend report function; compute counts/rates in SQL or application logic; return structured values; let the model explain them; include missing-data caveats.

Example input to the model: 100 attempted calls, 60 connected, 20 qualified. Connection rate=60/100=60%. Qualification per attempt=20/100=20%. Qualification per connection=20/60, about 33.3%. The wording must identify the denominator. These are teaching values, not your production results.
The strongest security point in your CV

The CV states that users only receive tools their JWT privileges allow and that the chatbot and API enforce the same RBAC rules. Explain both visibility and enforcement: a tool can be omitted from the available list, but backend checks still decide whether an attempted action is permitted.

Do not accept a model-proposed role, tenant or department as trusted. Revalidate scope in the service layer. Filter returned fields and use the same policy for exports, notifications and summaries. A model receiving forbidden data has already crossed the boundary even if a later prompt tells it not to reveal it.
Backend and UX choices

Why Flask rather than rebuilding in FastAPI? Existing functionality, team expertise and measured performance can justify staying with Flask. Why PostgreSQL rather than a vector store for reports? SQL handles joins, grouping and exact totals; vector similarity does not replace relational arithmetic. Why Socket.IO? It supports event- driven client updates such as job completion; durable status still needs a backend record.

Why both CSV and PDF? CSV supports further data analysis, while PDF supports readable summaries. Apply permission checks and data filtering consistently to both. Why pooled connections? Reuse reduces connection overhead and bounds resource usage, but pool size must be planned across processes.
Memory cue: Authorize -> query facts -> calculate -> explain -> notify/export safely.
Practice before reading the answers
E32.1: Why should a report assistant not estimate total revenue from loosely related retrieved documents?
E32.2: In the teaching counts, what is qualified-per-connected rate?
E32.3: Give a concise answer to "What makes your assistant more than a chatbot demo?"
Check your answers
E32.1: Authoritative structured data should be queried with explicit scope and calculations. Retrieval can provide context but cannot substitute for the actual financial records.
E32.2: 20/60, approximately 33.3%. It is different from 20% of all attempts.

E32.3: "It is integrated with live business reports and the application's permission model. Tools use authorized backend services, so the assistant explains real data without bypassing the same RBAC rules used by ordinary APIs."
Technical reading: [FLASK], [TOOLS], [SOCKETIO].

exercises.answer: "It is integrated with live business reports and the application's permission model. Tools use authorized backend services, so the assistant explains real data without bypassing the same RBAC rules used by ordinary APIs."
