definitions.definition: A network connects devices so they can exchange information.
definitions.example: Servers, workstations and cameras communicate through an organization's network.
definitions.note: Connectivity does not imply every device should be permitted to reach every other device.

definitions.definition: An IP address identifies a network interface within the relevant addressing and routing context.
definitions.example: A client sends packets toward a server's IP address.
definitions.note: Addresses can change, and one machine may have several interfaces or addresses.

definitions.definition: A transport-layer port helps identify an endpoint for communication on a host.
definitions.example: An HTTPS service commonly listens on TCP port 443.
definitions.note: A port number alone does not prove which trusted application is using it.

definitions.definition: DNS is a distributed naming system that resolves domain names into records such as IP addresses.
definitions.example: Resolve an API hostname before connecting to its server.
definitions.note: DNS resolution is distinct from successful authentication or an available API.

definitions.definition: A network switch connects devices and forwards frames within a network according to its capabilities and configuration.
definitions.example: Connect workstations and camera links in an office network.
definitions.note: Many switches have additional features; do not assume the CV's exact hardware or topology.

definitions.definition: A router forwards packets between networks according to routing information and policy.
definitions.example: Connect a local office network to another network or the internet.
definitions.note: Routing is not the same task as application-level authorization.

definitions.definition: A firewall enforces configured rules on network traffic.
definitions.example: Allow a database connection only from an approved backend network.
definitions.note: Permitted network traffic can still contain unsafe application requests.

definitions.definition: Bandwidth describes data-transmission capacity, usually in bits per second.
definitions.example: A 100-megabit-per-second link has a nominal capacity distinct from measured useful throughput.
definitions.note: Available throughput depends on overhead, contention and other constraints.

definitions.definition: Network latency is delay involved in delivering data over a communication path.
definitions.example: An API request experiences transit time before the server starts processing it.
definitions.note: High bandwidth does not necessarily mean low latency.

definitions.definition: CCTV refers to video monitoring delivered through a controlled system rather than general public broadcast.
definitions.example: The CV reports delivery of a 120-camera project.
definitions.note: The source does not identify its precise camera technology or storage configuration.

definitions.definition: An IP camera sends digital video using network communication.
definitions.example: A network camera streams video to an authorized recording system.
definitions.note: This defines the technology; it is not proof that every camera in your earlier project was this type.

definitions.definition: An NVR records and manages video streams from supported network cameras.
definitions.example: A recording service stores camera streams for later authorized review.
definitions.note: Retention, redundancy and access controls require separate design decisions.

definitions.definition: PoE provides power and data through supported Ethernet equipment and cabling.
definitions.example: A compatible switch powers a compatible camera through its network cable.
definitions.note: Device power requirements and the switch's total power budget still matter.

definitions.definition: A bit is a binary unit representing one of two values, conventionally 0 or 1.
definitions.example: Network rates are commonly expressed in millions of bits per second.
definitions.note: Do not confuse a bit with a byte when calculating storage.

definitions.definition: A byte conventionally contains eight bits in modern computing systems.
definitions.example: 240 megabits per second is 30 megabytes per second before additional considerations.
definitions.note: Decimal MB and binary MiB use different multipliers.

definitions.definition: Video retention is the policy and duration for keeping recordings before deletion or archival.
definitions.example: A hypothetical seven-day policy requires storage for seven days of expected video volume.
definitions.note: Do not invent the actual project's policy from its camera count.

definitions.definition: A capacity calculation estimates required resources from explicit workload assumptions.
definitions.example: At a hypothetical 2 Mb/s each, 120 cameras produce 240 Mb/s, or about 2.592 decimal TB per day before overhead.
definitions.note: These numbers illustrate arithmetic, not the specifications of the CV project.

definitions.definition: Network administration operates and maintains network services, devices and related infrastructure.
definitions.example: The CV describes managing company network and servers at Indus Dyeing.
definitions.note: It is technical experience but not automatically an equal number of software-engineering or LLM-production years.

definitions.definition: A research associate contributes to a research program under its defined scope and responsibilities.
definitions.example: The CV associates the NBIC Lab role with privacy-preserving machine learning and SMPC.
definitions.note: State your real contribution rather than inferring it solely from the lab or job title.

definitions.definition: A lead data analyst coordinates analytical work and communicates useful, supported findings.
definitions.example: The Wasaib Sanwaro role involved Power BI monitoring, analysis and audit reporting.
definitions.note: Analysis leadership should not be relabeled as a different engineering role without evidence.

definitions.definition: Freelance ML/data-science work delivers agreed analytical or model-related solutions for clients.
definitions.example: Your CV names pipelines, dashboards, retention analysis and YOLOv5 work during 2020-2022.
definitions.note: The source does not assign every deliverable to a specific named client.

definitions.definition: An MS is a master's-level qualification; the CV lists Computer Science at the Institute of Southern Punjab, 2024-2026.
definitions.example: Connect relevant computing foundations to a technical explanation you can demonstrate.
definitions.note: The source does not supply grades, a thesis title or every course taken.

definitions.definition: The CV lists a BS (Hons.) in Telecommunication Systems from Bahauddin Zakariya University, 2012-2016.
definitions.example: Relate communication concepts to networking and realtime system discussions.
definitions.note: Do not infer exact modules or qualification equivalence beyond the supplied record.

definitions.definition: The CV lists this Stanford University and DeepLearning.AI specialization via Coursera as a certification.
definitions.example: Revise supervised learning, evaluation and related concepts rather than reciting the certificate name alone.
definitions.note: A certificate does not by itself establish a specific production deployment.

definitions.term: Neural Networks and Deep Learning certification
definitions.definition: The CV lists this DeepLearning.AI certification via Coursera.
definitions.example: Use a small neural-network example to explain weights, loss and gradient-based learning.
definitions.note: Describe demonstrated understanding rather than inventing grades or dates.
aliases: Neural Networks and Deep Learning certification

definitions.definition: The CV lists IBM Cognitive Class's Machine Learning with Python, ML0101EN.
definitions.example: Connect Python-based model training and evaluation concepts to your real experience.
definitions.note: The certificate's name alone does not identify all tools used professionally.

definitions.definition: The CV reports a full CSC scholarship associated with the China research period.
definitions.example: Mention the scholarship as part of the documented academic and research story.
definitions.note: It is an award, not a substitute for explaining the actual research.

definitions.definition: Professional recognition is an award or acknowledgement of specified work or achievement.
definitions.example: The CV names an Indus Group recognition certificate and a Punjab academic laptop award.
definitions.note: Keep the description within the supplied evidence and do not invent ranking or selection statistics.

definitions.definition: Language proficiency describes a person's ability to communicate in a language.
definitions.example: The CV lists Urdu as native and English and Chinese as fluent.
definitions.note: Be ready to demonstrate the level claimed; no standardized test score is supplied.

definitions.definition: An experience timeline records dated roles and projects while distinguishing overlapping work.
definitions.example: The NBIC period overlaps the start of the freelance date range.
definitions.note: Do not add overlapping months twice or convert all technical work into production GenAI experience.

definitions.definition: An evidence boundary separates what a source establishes from what remains an example, inference or unknown.
definitions.example: The CV reports a speed improvement but not the exact index that achieved it.
definitions.note: An honest answer names the measured claim and retrieves missing implementation detail rather than inventing it.

questions.prompt: Which part of an application checks permissions and applies server-side business rules?
options: The backend
The browser layout
The JSON format
The visual theme
questions.explanation: The backend validates requests and enforces rules. The frontend displays and collects information; JSON carries data. A visual control is not a security check.
questions.hint: UI shows. API coordinates. Database remembers. Model assists. Backend authorizes.

questions.prompt: What is an API in the workbook's simplest explanation?
options: A graphical screen that only people can operate
A database that stores all application records
An agreed way for one piece of software to use another
The runtime that executes every programming language
questions.explanation: An API defines how software interacts. Storage is a database responsibility, a runtime executes code, and a screen is a user interface.
questions.hint: UI shows. API coordinates. Database remembers. Model assists. Backend authorizes.

questions.prompt: A user asks One System for a reporting total. Which order keeps the result authoritative?
options: UI displays all records, then hides unauthorized ones
Browser request, backend permission check, database query, JSON response, UI display
Browser guesses a total, then stores it in PostgreSQL
LLM invents a total, then the backend authorizes it
questions.explanation: The workbook's request flow checks access before retrieving permitted facts. React displays the result; an AI assistant can explain authorized data but is not the source of truth.
questions.hint: UI shows. API coordinates. Database remembers. Model assists. Backend authorizes.

questions.prompt: An operation takes two seconds, and the system completes 100 operations each second. What do these describe?
options: Availability and serialization
Latency and throughput, respectively
Throughput and latency, respectively
Concurrency and database durability
questions.explanation: Latency is elapsed time for one operation. Throughput is completions per time unit. Concurrency counts operations in progress, not finished operations.
questions.hint: UI shows. API coordinates. Database remembers. Model assists. Backend authorizes.

questions.prompt: An admin delete button is hidden for ordinary users. What additional control is essential?
options: A rule asking users not to call the endpoint
A less obvious button label
Backend authorization for the delete action and target record
A private frontend route name
questions.explanation: Users can bypass the UI and call an endpoint directly. The server must verify permission on both the operation and the specific object.
questions.hint: UI shows. API coordinates. Database remembers. Model assists. Backend authorizes.

questions.prompt: Your backend receives a browser request and then calls OpenAI. How should you describe its roles?
options: Server to the browser, client to OpenAI
Always a client because it uses the internet
A database in the first interaction and a runtime in the second
Always a server and never a client
questions.explanation: Client and server describe roles in an interaction. Receiving a request makes the backend a server in one conversation; initiating another makes it a client there.
questions.hint: UI shows. API coordinates. Database remembers. Model assists. Backend authorizes.

questions.prompt: Which Python collection maps keys to values?
options: A tuple
A list
A dictionary
A set
questions.explanation: A dictionary associates keys with values. Lists and tuples are ordered collections; a set stores distinct values for membership-oriented operations.
questions.hint: List orders; dictionary maps; set deduplicates; function organizes; exception reports failure.

questions.prompt: What does a Python type hint primarily provide?
options: An encryption rule for the value
An expected type for documentation and checking tools
A guarantee that no exception can occur
Automatic verification of all incoming HTTP bytes
questions.explanation: Ordinary Python does not enforce every hint at runtime. Untrusted input still needs parsing and validation. A hint is neither encryption nor an error-handling guarantee.
questions.hint: List orders; dictionary maps; set deduplicates; function organizes; exception reports failure.

questions.prompt: Why does the workbook's email example use both a set and a list?
options: The set sorts emails; the list prevents exceptions
The list verifies email ownership; the set encrypts addresses
The set checks membership; the list preserves first-occurrence order
Both are required for lowercasing strings
questions.explanation: The set tracks previously seen normalized values efficiently. The list preserves intentional output order. The example is a normalization policy, not full email validation.
questions.hint: List orders; dictionary maps; set deduplicates; function organizes; exception reports failure.

questions.prompt: The business wants repeated emails preserved. What changes in the deduplication example?
options: Catch all exceptions and return an empty list
Use a larger set so duplicates fit
Sort the input before running the same filter
Remove the seen-membership filter and append each nonempty normalized value
questions.explanation: Duplicate removal is a business decision. Keeping the membership filter would still remove repeats. A larger set or sorting does not change that rule.
questions.hint: List orders; dictionary maps; set deduplicates; function organizes; exception reports failure.

questions.prompt: For n inputs, what are the workbook deduplication example's expected time and extra space?
options: O(n) time and O(n) space
O(1) time and O(1) space
O(n squared) time and O(1) space
O(log n) time and O(log n) space
questions.explanation: It visits inputs once and uses expected constant-time set lookups. Stored seen values and output can grow with n. Actual constants and input sizes still matter.
questions.hint: List orders; dictionary maps; set deduplicates; function organizes; exception reports failure.

questions.prompt: Why not keep each request's customer records in one global mutable list?
options: Requests can leak state, and separate processes do not share it consistently
Python cannot store objects in lists
Lists require every request to be processed twice
Global lists automatically encrypt their contents
questions.explanation: The workbook warns that shared mutable state can cross request boundaries and is not automatically synchronized across processes. Keep request-local data local and persist shared facts appropriately.
questions.hint: List orders; dictionary maps; set deduplicates; function organizes; exception reports failure.

questions.prompt: Which definition describes concurrency?
options: Multiple tasks make overlapping progress
Every task executes on a separate CPU at the same instant
Every request is completed before another starts
All operations become durable when declared async
questions.explanation: Concurrency is overlapping progress; parallelism is simultaneous execution. Async scheduling can share waiting time but does not itself make work durable.
questions.hint: Async shares waiting time; workers isolate heavy work; queues preserve work.

questions.prompt: Which operation is usually I/O-bound from your application's perspective?
options: Sorting a large in-memory array
Calculating a large local model's outputs
Running a long synchronous Python calculation
Waiting for a remote model API response
questions.explanation: A remote call spends time waiting for an external service. Local calculations use compute. The same embedding task can be I/O-bound remotely and compute-heavy locally.
questions.hint: Async shares waiting time; workers isolate heavy work; queues preserve work.

questions.prompt: An async endpoint uses time.sleep(5) only to create a delay. What is the appropriate nonblocking replacement?
options: await asyncio.sleep(5)
Removing await from all network calls
A longer time.sleep call
A synchronous loop that checks the clock
questions.explanation: asyncio.sleep yields control while the timer waits. time.sleep blocks the event-loop thread. This change fixes that timer, not other blocking work in the endpoint.
questions.hint: Async shares waiting time; workers isolate heavy work; queues preserve work.

questions.prompt: What is the purpose of a semaphore around outgoing API calls?
options: Replace all database permission checks
Persist jobs after process restart
Make every response correct
Limit the number of operations entering that section together
questions.explanation: A semaphore controls concurrent work. It can protect dependency capacity, but it does not provide correctness, persistence or authorization by itself.
questions.hint: Async shares waiting time; workers isolate heavy work; queues preserve work.

questions.prompt: A two-minute report must finish even if the web process restarts. Which design fits?
options: Keep the report in a global list without persistence
Only call asyncio.create_task in the web process
Wait in the browser until the process returns
Persist a job in a durable queue and expose job status
questions.explanation: In-memory tasks can disappear with their process. The workbook recommends durable jobs, status tracking and retry-safe workers for restart-surviving work.
questions.hint: Async shares waiting time; workers isolate heavy work; queues preserve work.

questions.prompt: An async service freezes while a large Python calculation runs. Which response matches the workbook?
options: Move heavy work to suitable processes, specialized libraries or a worker service
Add async to the function name and change nothing inside
Launch unlimited additional coroutines
Increase only the HTTP response timeout
questions.explanation: Async does not offload CPU work automatically. Isolating heavy computation and bounding work protects latency-sensitive requests; a longer timeout hides the symptom.
questions.hint: Async shares waiting time; workers isolate heavy work; queues preserve work.

questions.prompt: Which pairing is correct?
options: TypeScript is a queue; JavaScript is a cloud service
Node.js is a database; TypeScript is a browser
JavaScript is a language; Node.js is a runtime
JavaScript is a framework; Node.js is a type checker
questions.explanation: The workbook separates language, runtime and static type system. Node runs JavaScript outside the browser; TypeScript adds static type checking.
questions.hint: JavaScript is the language; Node is the runtime; TypeScript checks contracts before runtime.

questions.prompt: What does a Promise represent?
options: A future completion or failure
A guaranteed separate CPU thread
A database transaction that cannot fail
A permanent storage record
questions.explanation: Promises represent asynchronous outcomes. They do not inherently provide transactions, separate compute resources or persistence.
questions.hint: JavaScript is the language; Node is the runtime; TypeScript checks contracts before runtime.

questions.prompt: What does parseCount("12") return in the workbook's TypeScript example?
options: The string unchanged with ok: true
An error because the input is a string, not an integer number
A database insertion
The integer 12 through automatic coercion
questions.explanation: The example checks typeof and Number.isInteger. It deliberately does not coerce strings; parseCount(-1) fails a separate nonnegative rule.
questions.hint: JavaScript is the language; Node is the runtime; TypeScript checks contracts before runtime.

questions.prompt: In Result<T>, why check result.ok before reading result.value?
options: It encrypts the successful result
It moves processing to a worker
It converts every string to T
It identifies which union variant is present
questions.explanation: The ok field discriminates the success and failure shapes. Checking it narrows the type; value belongs to the successful branch.
questions.hint: JavaScript is the language; Node is the runtime; TypeScript checks contracts before runtime.

questions.prompt: Why is response as number insufficient for an untrusted API response?
options: TypeScript refuses all network requests
Casts automatically change database permissions
A numeric type makes invalid data impossible
A cast does not inspect or validate the runtime value
questions.explanation: Static declarations and assertions cannot establish that external bytes match a type. Validate at the trust boundary, then use static contracts within the program.
questions.hint: JavaScript is the language; Node is the runtime; TypeScript checks contracts before runtime.

questions.prompt: Which is the defensible reason to consider TypeScript for TableOS?
options: TypeScript is always faster than Python for every workload
Node.js guarantees unlimited capacity in a single process
TypeScript makes authorization unnecessary
Shared frontend/backend contracts and tooling, balanced against typing and build overhead
questions.explanation: The workbook presents shared language and contracts as a rationale to verify against actual decisions. It explicitly avoids claiming inherent scalability superiority over Python.
questions.hint: JavaScript is the language; Node is the runtime; TypeScript checks contracts before runtime.

questions.prompt: What is OpenAPI?
options: A user authentication token
A database engine
A Python server framework
A machine-readable description of API operations and schemas
questions.explanation: OpenAPI describes a contract. FastAPI, Flask and Fastify execute application code. A documented contract still needs matching implementation and tests.
questions.hint: HTTP transports; REST organizes; OpenAPI describes; frameworks execute; schemas validate.

questions.prompt: Which status commonly means work was accepted for asynchronous processing?
questions.explanation: 202 communicates accepted work, often with a job ID or status location. 201 means created, 403 forbidden, and 429 rate limited.
questions.hint: HTTP transports; REST organizes; OpenAPI describes; frameworks execute; schemas validate.

questions.prompt: A Pydantic-valid request asks for another tenant's report. What should happen next?
options: Ask the frontend to hide the report after returning it
Allow it because the schema passed
Let the LLM decide whether the tenant looks trustworthy
Reject it if backend authorization does not permit that report
questions.explanation: Validation checks shape and values. Authorization checks rights to the specific resource. They solve different problems.
questions.hint: HTTP transports; REST organizes; OpenAPI describes; frameworks execute; schemas validate.

questions.prompt: Which stack correctly matches the workbook?
options: FastAPI and Flask use Python; Fastify uses Node.js
Fastify and Flask are vector databases
Pydantic is a frontend styling library
OpenAPI is a replacement for all three frameworks
questions.explanation: FastAPI and Flask are Python web frameworks, Fastify is a Node framework, and Pydantic provides structured runtime data validation.
questions.hint: HTTP transports; REST organizes; OpenAPI describes; frameworks execute; schemas validate.

questions.prompt: A Flask endpoint is slow because of its database query. What is the sound first action?
options: Rewrite it in FastAPI and assume latency is fixed
Remove validation to hide the delay
Measure the query and dependency bottleneck before choosing a change
Add more API documentation and stop measuring
questions.explanation: Framework replacement does not repair a slow query, blocking dependency or exhausted pool. The workbook recommends the smallest effective improvement after measurement.
questions.hint: HTTP transports; REST organizes; OpenAPI describes; frameworks execute; schemas validate.

questions.prompt: A Pydantic field has min_length=1. Why can a string of spaces still pass?
options: Pydantic never validates strings
Length is not the same as nonblank content
OpenAPI removes all string rules
Spaces automatically become a database error
questions.explanation: The sample deliberately notes that minimum length alone accepts spaces. A nonblank policy requires an additional check such as trimming and validating content.
questions.hint: HTTP transports; REST organizes; OpenAPI describes; frameworks execute; schemas validate.

questions.prompt: What does a foreign key do?
options: Encrypts a table column
Makes every value globally unique
Constrains a reference to a related row according to database rules
Replaces the need for a primary key in all tables
questions.explanation: A foreign key enforces a relationship. A primary key identifies a row. These constraints do not encrypt data.
questions.hint: Rows represent things; keys identify/link them; joins combine; transactions protect changes.

questions.prompt: Which description fits Kysely?
options: An authentication protocol
A type-safe TypeScript SQL query builder
A separate database engine
An automatic performance optimizer
questions.explanation: Kysely helps compose SQL with type information. You still need to understand joins, indexes, transactions and tenant scoping.
questions.hint: Rows represent things; keys identify/link them; joins combine; transactions protect changes.

questions.prompt: After a LEFT JOIN, a customer with no matching calls appears once with NULL call fields. How should you count matching calls?
options: SUM(customers.id)
COUNT(customers.name)
COUNT(calls.id), using a nonnullable call identifier
COUNT(*)
questions.explanation: COUNT(*) counts the preserved left-side row. Counting the right-side non-NULL identifier produces zero when no call matched.
questions.hint: Rows represent things; keys identify/link them; joins combine; transactions protect changes.

questions.prompt: A record change and its audit insert must both succeed or neither should persist. What is appropriate?
options: An LLM instruction saying they are atomic
Two unrelated writes with no rollback
A frontend loading indicator
One database transaction containing both operations
questions.explanation: Atomicity groups database writes into all-or-nothing work. Error handling must roll back failures rather than report partial success.
questions.hint: Rows represent things; keys identify/link them; joins combine; transactions protect changes.

questions.prompt: Where does the workbook put calls.status='completed' to preserve customers with no completed calls?
options: In the SELECT column label
Only in WHERE after the join
In ORDER BY
In the LEFT JOIN ON condition
questions.explanation: Putting the right-side filter in ON limits matches without removing the preserved left-side row. A WHERE filter on that field would remove unmatched rows.
questions.hint: Rows represent things; keys identify/link them; joins combine; transactions protect changes.

questions.prompt: A typed query builder produced a query. Which concerns still require engineering review?
options: Only variable spelling
None, because type-safe means tenant-safe
Only whether the frontend uses React
Performance, tenant filters and authorization
questions.explanation: A query builder helps with syntax and known types. It cannot prove the query is efficient or that a caller has access to the returned data.
questions.hint: Rows represent things; keys identify/link them; joins combine; transactions protect changes.

questions.prompt: Why can JSONB suit an Airtable-class platform?
options: It makes all data automatically public
It removes the need for validation
It prevents every possible query slowdown
It supports flexible user-defined fields alongside stable relational metadata
questions.explanation: Hybrid storage combines stable relational columns with flexible JSONB values. Querying and validation still require deliberate design.
questions.hint: Measure -> inspect plan -> change one cause -> remeasure -> verify correct results.

questions.prompt: What is a database index?
options: An additional structure that helps locate matching rows
A second name for every database transaction
A replacement for all stored records
A guarantee that all queries avoid scanning
questions.explanation: Indexes speed suitable access patterns but consume storage and add write maintenance. A query must be compatible with the index to benefit.
questions.hint: Measure -> inspect plan -> change one cause -> remeasure -> verify correct results.

questions.prompt: Four API replicas each allow 25 database connections. What is their combined maximum before workers and administration?
questions.explanation: Pool sizes multiply across replicas. Plan capacity across the complete deployment rather than sizing one process in isolation.
questions.hint: Measure -> inspect plan -> change one cause -> remeasure -> verify correct results.

questions.prompt: What does EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) do that ordinary EXPLAIN does not?
options: Guarantees zero production load
Only changes SQL formatting
Creates all missing indexes
Executes the statement and reports observed work
questions.explanation: ANALYZE executes the statement, including writes. Inspect representative plans safely; even a heavy read can load production.
questions.hint: Measure -> inspect plan -> change one cause -> remeasure -> verify correct results.

questions.prompt: Does a generic GIN index on JSONB guarantee data::text ILIKE '%abc%' will be fast?
options: No index can ever help any text search
Yes; every JSON expression uses every GIN index
No; index usability depends on the expression and operators
Yes; casting JSONB to text disables all scanning
questions.explanation: The workbook requires checking the actual plan. A suitable index or search representation is a hypothesis to measure, not a universal fix.
questions.hint: Measure -> inspect plan -> change one cause -> remeasure -> verify correct results.

questions.prompt: Which statement stays within the CV evidence for the 60+ second to 1-2 second improvement?
options: The change eliminated every database bottleneck
I proved a particular GIN index was the sole cause, without checking records
Every query in TableOS now has a 1-second P95
I rewrote the query path and tuned PostgreSQL; I must verify the precise index and benchmark details
questions.explanation: The CV supports the measured outcome and broad method, not an exact index or percentile. Separate verified history from proposed techniques.
questions.hint: Measure -> inspect plan -> change one cause -> remeasure -> verify correct results.

questions.prompt: Which pairing is correct?
options: A queue guarantees every external effect happens only once
A queue grants user permissions; a worker stores JWTs
A worker is always the user's browser
A queue holds work; a worker executes it
questions.explanation: Queues decouple waiting work from execution. Workers process jobs; duplicate-safe effects and permissions require additional controls.
questions.hint: Queue remembers work; worker performs it; retry repeats; idempotency prevents duplicate effects; outbox ties events to committed facts.

questions.prompt: What does idempotency mean here?
options: The system has no retries
Repeating the same logical operation has the same intended effect
Every network request always succeeds
The function can never run twice
questions.explanation: Idempotency concerns effects, not execution count. A retry can run again without producing another unintended business effect.
questions.hint: Queue remembers work; worker performs it; retry repeats; idempotency prevents duplicate effects; outbox ties events to committed facts.

questions.prompt: A relay publishes an outbox event and crashes before marking it sent. What must the design tolerate?
options: The database automatically recalling the published message
All future events being impossible to publish
The external API joining the original SQL transaction
The event being published again
questions.explanation: Recovery can publish the same event again. Consumers must recognize the logical operation and handle duplicates safely.
questions.hint: Queue remembers work; worker performs it; retry repeats; idempotency prevents duplicate effects; outbox ties events to committed facts.

questions.prompt: What is wrong with using only report:monthly for private reports across all tenants?
options: The key automatically expires immediately
Redis cannot store text keys
The key is too long for any database
Different tenants can receive the same cached private data
questions.explanation: Cache identity must include relevant tenant/user scope and parameters. Cache hits must not bypass permission checks.
questions.hint: Queue remembers work; worker performs it; retry repeats; idempotency prevents duplicate effects; outbox ties events to committed facts.

questions.prompt: Why write a business change and an outbox event in one SQL transaction?
options: So every external API becomes part of the SQL transaction
So the queue becomes the only source of business truth
So the event record and business change commit together, closing the dual-write gap
So workers never need retries
questions.explanation: The outbox ties an event to committed facts. Publication happens later and can repeat; it does not make an unrelated external side effect atomic.
questions.hint: Queue remembers work; worker performs it; retry repeats; idempotency prevents duplicate effects; outbox ties events to committed facts.

questions.prompt: A processed_events table is written separately from sending an email. Is that sufficient to guarantee one email?
options: No; the email and marker can fail independently, so use supported idempotency or reconciliation
Yes; any local table provides an eternal external guarantee
Yes; removing completed queue jobs prevents all duplication
No; retries are never appropriate anywhere
questions.explanation: An ambiguous external outcome can lead to a duplicate send. A local marker alone cannot atomically control an unrelated provider's effect.
questions.hint: Queue remembers work; worker performs it; retry repeats; idempotency prevents duplicate effects; outbox ties events to committed facts.

questions.prompt: What describes a modular monolith?
options: A system with no modules or separation
An application with explicit internal boundaries without making each module a network service
One database for every function call
A guarantee that all code must run in one process forever
questions.explanation: The workbook distinguishes logical modules from independently deployed services. Clear boundaries do not require premature microservice deployment.
questions.hint: Requirements first; boundaries second; deployment topology third.

questions.prompt: What is a tenant in a multi-tenant SaaS system?
options: A customer organization or other isolation unit
A database index type
Every individual HTTP response
The model provider's token limit
questions.explanation: Tenants can share infrastructure while access and resource use remain separated. Isolation must extend beyond database queries.
questions.hint: Requirements first; boundaries second; deployment topology third.

questions.prompt: A CRM update may take 20 seconds after a user edits a record. What fits the workbook's design?
options: Make record edits depend on Slack availability
Tell the user everything is synchronized as soon as the local save succeeds
Commit the local edit and outbox event, then sync in a worker with visible status
Hold the database transaction open until the CRM replies
questions.explanation: Local commit and external synchronization have different consistency boundaries. Expose pending/completed/failed status honestly and recover asynchronously.
questions.hint: Requirements first; boundaries second; deployment topology third.

questions.prompt: Does a monorepo prove an application is a monolith?
options: No; repository organization and deployment architecture are separate choices
Yes; multiple services require separate languages
No; a monorepo proves the system uses microservices
Yes; one repository can only produce one process
questions.explanation: One repository can contain multiple deployed services. A modular monolith describes architectural boundaries, not merely repository layout.
questions.hint: Requirements first; boundaries second; deployment topology third.

questions.prompt: When is extracting a module into a microservice most defensible?
options: Whenever a new framework becomes fashionable
Whenever a module has more than one file
When distinct scaling needs, a stable contract and ownership outweigh operational complexity
Before any requirements are known
questions.explanation: The workbook weighs benefit against network failures, tracing, retries and deployment coordination. More services are not automatically a better design.
questions.hint: Requirements first; boundaries second; deployment topology third.

questions.prompt: Where must tenant scope be considered besides SQL queries?
options: Nowhere once a tenant_id field exists
Only the frontend theme
Only the application name
Caches, search indexes, object storage paths and background jobs
questions.explanation: Tenant isolation is a cross-cutting rule. Resolve allowed scope from authenticated membership and carry it through all data-access paths.
questions.hint: Requirements first; boundaries second; deployment topology third.

questions.prompt: Which question is answered by authorization?
options: What may this identity do?
How many tokens fit in a model?
What color should the login screen be?
Who is this identity?
questions.explanation: Authentication establishes identity; authorization checks permitted operations and resources. An authenticated user can still be forbidden from a record.
questions.hint: Authenticate the identity; authorize the action, resource and field; audit the outcome.

questions.prompt: Does signing an ordinary JWT encrypt its payload?
options: Only if the user has an admin role
No; the payload remains readable
Only when it is sent in JSON
Yes; every signed JWT is encrypted
questions.explanation: A signature protects integrity. Do not put passwords or other secrets in ordinary readable token claims.
questions.hint: Authenticate the identity; authorize the action, resource and field; audit the outcome.

questions.prompt: A user may read a report but not salary fields. Should the AI report tool reveal salaries?

Flask routing by itself
The OpenAI embedding model
A CSS stylesheet
questions.explanation: Embeddings create numerical representations, ChromaDB stores/retrieves them, Flask serves the application and GPT-4 generates answers from selected context.
questions.hint: Transcribe accurately; preserve who/when/negation; structure only supported facts; require review.

questions.prompt: What does SOAP stand for in the workbook's documentation project?
options: Subjective, Objective, Assessment and Plan
Search, Optimize, Analyze and Publish
Storage, Output, API and Permissions
Speech, Objects, Audio and Prompts
questions.explanation: SOAP structures clinical notes. This describes documentation roles, not permission for an AI to diagnose or invent clinical observations.
questions.hint: Transcribe accurately; preserve who/when/negation; structure only supported facts; require review.

questions.prompt: A transcript gives no temperature measurement. Should the note say 'Temperature normal'?
options: Yes; a valid JSON schema supplies missing facts
No; keep it not documented under the agreed schema
Yes; absence of a statement proves normality
Only if the model has high confidence
questions.explanation: Not mentioned is not the same as normal or absent. Generated notes must preserve missingness rather than fabricate measurements.
questions.hint: Transcribe accurately; preserve who/when/negation; structure only supported facts; require review.

questions.prompt: The transcript mentions a headache and a Friday follow-up, but no exam or diagnosis. What is appropriate?
options: Record the stated symptom and plan while leaving unsupported findings unfilled
Invent a routine examination so every section looks complete
Infer a medication from similar cases
Treat the follow-up date as a diagnosis
questions.explanation: The workbook's teaching example structures only source-supported facts. Completeness of a form does not justify unsupported content.
questions.hint: Transcribe accurately; preserve who/when/negation; structure only supported facts; require review.

questions.prompt: Why is valid SOAP JSON insufficient to prove a good note?
options: JSON always guarantees correct meaning
It can still reverse negation, misattribute speakers or invent facts
A schema checks the clinician's actual intent automatically
Formatting is the only concern in transcription
questions.explanation: Verify claims against source audio/transcript, including speaker, time and negation, and retain qualified review. Structural validity is only one layer.
questions.hint: Transcribe accurately; preserve who/when/negation; structure only supported facts; require review.

questions.prompt: What does a public ChromaDocBot repository establish by itself?
options: A verified regulatory certification
Visible project code, not proof that every shown feature ran at production scale
A verified uptime history
Exact production concurrency limits
questions.explanation: The workbook separates code availability from deployment evidence. Verify chunk sizes, topology, access model and evaluation results from actual project records.
questions.hint: Transcribe accurately; preserve who/when/negation; structure only supported facts; require review.

questions.prompt: Which description matches the workbook?
options: A manifest is the entire running backend
A skill is always a trained model; a plugin is always a database
A marketplace is a private encryption key
A skill packages reusable task instructions; a plugin packages installable capabilities
questions.explanation: Skills, plugins, marketplaces and manifests are different packaging/distribution layers. Use each term for its specific role.
questions.hint: Source -> inventory -> validate -> attribute -> package -> test -> publish.

questions.prompt: What does the CV claim about the 985 Skills Stack skills?
options: Training 985 separate models
Curation, packaging and tooling, not sole authorship of every upstream skill
Building 985 cloud data centers
Personal authorship of every upstream instruction
questions.explanation: Credit upstream authors. The engineering contribution includes inventory, classification, deduplication, attribution, manifests and catalog generation.
questions.hint: Source -> inventory -> validate -> attribute -> package -> test -> publish.

questions.prompt: Can valid JSON describe a broken plugin?
options: Only if the file is larger than a model context window
No; JSON syntax proves installability
No; every path in JSON exists automatically
Yes; paths, semantics or compatibility can still be wrong
questions.explanation: Syntax is only one check. Validate referenced files, required semantics and actual discovery/installation behavior.
questions.hint: Source -> inventory -> validate -> attribute -> package -> test -> publish.

questions.prompt: Why track an upstream revision as well as a repository name?
options: To identify exactly which version was reviewed and packaged
To replace all license review
To guarantee there can never be updates
To avoid crediting the source
questions.explanation: Version identity helps reproduce packages, investigate security changes and manage updates and attribution.
questions.hint: Source -> inventory -> validate -> attribute -> package -> test -> publish.

questions.prompt: Why can a GitHub Pages catalog need a separate backend for some features?
options: Static pages cannot display text
A catalog automatically includes a private API server
Client-side searching requires an SQL server in every browser
Static hosting does not itself run arbitrary server-side operations
questions.explanation: A static catalog can search generated data in the browser. Server-side secrets, live operations or some shared state require another service.
questions.hint: Source -> inventory -> validate -> attribute -> package -> test -> publish.

questions.prompt: Why review a third-party skill before using it with a powerful agent?
options: Every publicly visible file has unrestricted reuse rights
A friendly title is proof of safety
Its instructions or scripts may cause commands, file access or credential exposure
A valid manifest guarantees safe behavior
questions.explanation: The workbook calls for reviewing content/dependencies, respecting licenses and limiting permissions. Discoverability and installability are not safety guarantees.
questions.hint: Source -> inventory -> validate -> attribute -> package -> test -> publish.

questions.prompt: What does secure multiparty computation enable under a defined threat model?
options: Only local browser state management
A guarantee that outputs reveal nothing in every situation
Joint computation of agreed results while protecting private inputs
Automatic publication of all raw records
questions.explanation: MPC guarantees depend on protocol and adversary assumptions. Released results can still disclose information, so output policy remains important.
questions.hint: Research answer = problem + method + comparison + evidence + limitation + your contribution.

questions.prompt: What does a low-resource language setting mean here?
options: Limited suitable data, benchmarks or tooling for the task
A language with less complexity or importance
A requirement that every model must be trained from scratch
A language that cannot be tokenized
questions.explanation: The term concerns available resources, not linguistic worth. Urdu tasks may need attention to script variation, code-switching and dataset quality.
questions.hint: Research answer = problem + method + comparison + evidence + limitation + your contribution.

questions.prompt: Does federated learning automatically guarantee complete privacy?
options: Yes; distributed data always prevents leakage
Only if all participants use the same UI
Yes; it is identical to every MPC protocol
No; model updates or outputs may leak information
questions.explanation: Distributed training and formal privacy protections address different issues. Analyze the threat model and any additional safeguards.
questions.hint: Research answer = problem + method + comparison + evidence + limitation + your contribution.

questions.prompt: Can a paper title prove a numerical accuracy improvement?
options: Yes; every title includes a hidden metric
No; the actual methods and results must be consulted
Yes; the venue supplies the result automatically
Only if the title includes RAG
questions.explanation: The workbook has titles, venues and years, not datasets or experiments. Prepare real details from the papers rather than inventing them.
questions.hint: Research answer = problem + method + comparison + evidence + limitation + your contribution.

questions.prompt: Before claiming an MPC system is secure, what must you identify?
options: Only the number of lines of code
Only the model family
Participants, protected inputs, outputs, adversary behavior and collusion assumptions
Only the conference title
questions.explanation: Security is relative to specified assumptions and guarantees. A semi-honest participant differs from a malicious one that can deviate from the protocol.
questions.hint: Research answer = problem + method + comparison + evidence + limitation + your contribution.

questions.prompt: What is a strong research explanation?
options: Only the publication title read aloud
Only the latest model's name
An invented dataset size with a confident tone
Problem, method, comparison, evidence, limitation and personal contribution
questions.explanation: A baseline makes improvement meaningful, an ablation isolates contributions, and real data/configuration support reproducibility. State what your own work contributed.
questions.hint: Research answer = problem + method + comparison + evidence + limitation + your contribution.

questions.prompt: Which distinction is correct?
options: HLD explains major components and flows; LLD specifies detailed interfaces and behavior
HLD is CSS; LLD is a model token limit
LLD replaces every test automatically
Both mean only a list of libraries
questions.explanation: High-level structure needs lower-level contracts for validation, state transitions and failures. Architecture documents should make assumptions explicit.
questions.hint: Make decisions explicit; make work testable; make teammates stronger; make claims verifiable.

questions.prompt: What are acceptance criteria?
options: Observable conditions that define when work is complete
A list of tools without expected behavior
A promise that no future bug can exist
A developer's preferred font size only
questions.explanation: Concrete criteria make implementation testable. They should cover relevant normal and failure cases, not just code completion.
questions.hint: Make decisions explicit; make work testable; make teammates stronger; make claims verifiable.

questions.prompt: For a restart-safe CSV import, which detail belongs in LLD/contracts rather than only an HLD diagram?
options: Only the team headcount
Row-error formats, checkpoints, idempotency and validation limits
Only a list of external logos
Only the application's business name
questions.explanation: The HLD locates responsibilities; detailed contracts define exactly what happens when data is invalid, processing restarts or a retry occurs.
questions.hint: Make decisions explicit; make work testable; make teammates stronger; make claims verifiable.

questions.prompt: Which sequence is the workbook's reusable decision pattern?
options: Code count, salary, UI theme
Decision first, then omit alternatives
Brand name, confidence, more brand names
Problem, constraints, options, decision, trade-off, evidence
questions.explanation: Explain the actual need and constraints, compare reasonable choices, admit the cost and support the result with verified evidence.
questions.hint: Make decisions explicit; make work testable; make teammates stronger; make claims verifiable.

questions.prompt: An engineer proposes a different approach. What is a constructive response?
options: Select whichever tool has the newest name
Reject it only because your title is senior
Compare requirements and safety, test uncertain claims and document the reasoning
Avoid acceptance tests so disagreement stays subjective
questions.explanation: Technical leadership develops judgment and independence. Evidence and explicit trade-offs are more useful than authority alone.
questions.hint: Make decisions explicit; make work testable; make teammates stronger; make claims verifiable.

questions.prompt: Which wording fits architecting a project with a team?
options: Claim every contribution as personal code
Avoid discussing any responsibility
Distinguish what I designed, implemented, co-built and reviewed
Use 'we' to imply experience with unverified components
questions.explanation: The CV says architected and co-built. Strong senior positioning connects real ownership to clear evidence without appropriating all team work.
questions.hint: Make decisions explicit; make work testable; make teammates stronger; make claims verifiable.

questions.prompt: Which component forwards traffic between networks?
options: A stylesheet
A tokenizer
A DataFrame
A router
questions.explanation: The workbook contrasts switches within a local network, routers between networks, DNS for names and firewalls for traffic rules.
questions.hint: Present the progression: infrastructure -> research/data -> ML applications -> production AI/platform leadership.

questions.prompt: Which distinction is correct?
options: Bandwidth is transmission capacity; latency is delay
Latency is always a percentage
Bandwidth is delay; latency is a camera count
Both are the same as storage capacity
questions.explanation: Keep units and meanings distinct. Networking experience transfers usefully to realtime systems, but it is not the same role as LLM engineering.
questions.hint: Present the progression: infrastructure -> research/data -> ML applications -> production AI/platform leadership.

questions.prompt: Ten cameras each average 4 megabits per second. What is aggregate traffic before overhead?
options: 40 megabits/second, or 5 megabytes/second
40 megabytes/second
4 megabits/second
400 megabytes/second
questions.explanation: Multiply camera count by bitrate, then divide bits by eight for bytes. These are workbook teaching values, not verified specifications of the historical project.
questions.hint: Present the progression: infrastructure -> research/data -> ML applications -> production AI/platform leadership.

questions.prompt: Does network administration automatically count as production LLM engineering?
options: No; explain transferable skills while keeping role categories accurate
Yes; the earlier date proves longer LLM experience
Only if the network included cameras
Yes; all technical work has the same responsibilities
questions.explanation: The workbook distinguishes infrastructure, research/data, ML applications and production AI leadership. Do not relabel all technical employment into one category.
questions.hint: Present the progression: infrastructure -> research/data -> ML applications -> production AI/platform leadership.

questions.prompt: Research and freelance work overlap in the CV. How should years of experience be presented?
options: Count each overlapping month twice as elapsed time
Use an accurate dated timeline rather than adding overlapping months as sequential
Delete the earlier role from the story
Treat every role since 2016 as full-time backend engineering
questions.explanation: Explain the actual work and dates. Broad ML/applied-AI experience is not identical to years of full-time backend or production LLM deployment.
questions.hint: Present the progression: infrastructure -> research/data -> ML applications -> production AI/platform leadership.

questions.prompt: You are asked for a client-specific result absent from the CV. What is the reliable answer?
options: Borrow another client's result
Assign a plausible project to that client without checking
Treat a certification as proof of that deployment
Use actual records or say the precise detail needs verification
questions.explanation: The workbook preserves the named history but does not assign unseen deliverables, datasets or metrics. Honest boundaries protect credibility.
questions.hint: Present the progression: infrastructure -> research/data -> ML applications -> production AI/platform leadership.
